sens: Loud and resounding noise, like that of crackling flames or whistling wind
Sound wave of a destructive force
G4500.detail:
1. The word primarily evokes an intense and deafening noise, that of roaring flames or an object slicing through the air with a whistle. It is the very sound of destruction in progress. In 2 Peter 3:10, the heavens do not disappear in silence: they dissolve "with a crash," as if the entire universe is crying out as it disintegrates.
2. More broadly, this crash symbolizes the sudden and uncontrollable eruption of a power that overturns everything. The noise is not incidental: it expresses the overwhelming reality of what is happening, impossible to ignore or deny.
G4500.origine: The word comes from the Greek rhoïzos, which referred to the whistling of an arrow slicing through the air or the crackling of flames. The adverb rhoizèdon ("with this whistling, this crash") is constructed from this root: it paints the sound alongside the action. It is a rare word in the Greek Bible, coined to convey the violence of the moment.
G4500.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Peter 3:10. The Apostle Peter places it at the heart of his description of the final judgment: the heavens and the elements of the universe will not dissipate quietly, but will vanish with a crashing sound. This choice of word anchors the eschatological scene in a concrete sensory experience, making the final moment both terrible and irrevocable.
G4500.portee: This word reminds the reader that the end of the world will not be a distant abstraction, but a tangible and irrevocable event, heralding God's judgment with a force that no one can ignore. It invites one to take seriously the promises and warnings of Scripture, rather than living in carelessness.

sens: Sharp and pointed combat weapon, large and broad, used in close combat
Instrument of death and divine judgment
Word of God that judges and divides
G4501.detail:
1. The sword (rhomphaia) is primarily a weapon of war, a large double-edged blade used in hand-to-hand combat. It is a fearsome and deadly weapon: in Revelation 6:8, men perish by the sword, famine, and death.
2. The sword symbolizes God's judgment and destructive power. In Revelation, it comes out of the mouth of the glorified Christ (Revelation 1:16 and 19:15) to strike the nations and execute divine justice.
3. The sword can also represent the word of God that pierces the soul and reveals the hidden thoughts of the heart. In Luke 2:35, Simeon predicts to Mary that "a sword will pierce your soul," an image of the suffering that the passion of her Son will cause her, and a symbol of the separation that faith in Jesus creates.
G4501.origine: The word rhomphaia originally refers to a broad sword used by the Thracians, ancient warriors of the Balkans. It generally corresponds to the Hebrew "cherev" (sword) in the Greek translations of the Old Testament. The word is close to machaira (another Greek word for sword), but rhomphaia evokes more the large blade of barbarian warriors, while machaira is more general. In the Greek Bible, the two terms are often interchangeable.
G4501.emploi: The word appears 7 times in the Bible, only in the New Testament: once in Luke (2:35) and six times in Revelation. In Luke 2:35, it is an image of spiritual pain: the sword of suffering will pierce Mary's soul. In Revelation, the word takes on a cosmic and eschatological dimension: it embodies the power of the risen Christ (Revelation 1:16 and 2:12), His judgment on the nations (Revelation 19:15), and the plagues of the last day (Revelation 6:8). The sword is always associated with Christ or divine judgment, never with a mere human weapon.
G4501.portee: This word invites the reader to be aware that the word of Christ is alive and powerful: it judges the hidden thoughts of the heart (Luke 2:35), it separates, it divides. It leaves no one indifferent. For the Christian, this "sword" also reminds that the return of Christ in glory will be accompanied by a fearsome judgment, and that faith in Jesus, while bringing life, also entails a radical break with the old world.

sens: Firstborn son of Jacob and Leah
Tribe of Israel descended from this son
In Revelation, group of the elect marked with the divine seal
G4502.detail: 1. Reuben is the name of Jacob's firstborn son, born of Leah. According to the Old Testament, he is the ancestor of one of the twelve tribes of Israel. 2. The tribe of Reuben designates the entire people descended from this son, established east of the Jordan in the Promised Land. 3. In Revelation 7:5, Reuben represents one of the twelve spiritual tribes of Israel whose twelve thousand members receive the seal of God on their foreheads, symbolizing their protection and belonging to the chosen people in the last days.
G4502.origine: The name Reuben comes from the Hebrew "Re'uben," which literally means "behold, a son" (from "re" = behold, and "ben" = son). It thus carries the sense of joy or an exclamation at the birth of the firstborn. This Hebrew name is directly transliterated into Greek as "Ῥουβήν" in the Greek texts of the New Testament.
G4502.emploi: Reuben appears only once in the New Testament, in Revelation 7:5, where the Apostle John lists the twelve tribes of Israel in his vision of the elect marked with the seal. Here, Reuben represents one of the twelve traditional tribes, taken up in a context of eschatological salvation — that is, the final fulfillment of God's promises to His people. The apocalyptic context gives this ancient name a new and spiritual significance in the mystery of the coming Kingdom.
G4502.portee: For the Christian reader, the mention of Reuben in Revelation recalls the continuity between historical Israel and God's eternal salvific plan. It signifies that the people of God, though tested, remain the object of His protection and love, sealed and destined for eternal glory. This name also evokes the heritage of faith granted to those who believe in Christ.

sens: Moabite woman, ancestor of David and Jesus
G4503.detail: Ruth is a woman from Moab who, after the death of her first husband, remains faithful to her mother-in-law Naomi and returns with her to Israel. She marries Boaz, a good man from Bethlehem, and becomes the ancestor of King David and, thus, of Jesus Himself (Matthew 1:5).
G4503.origine: The name Ruth comes from the Hebrew רוּת (Ruth), whose exact etymology remains debated, but which could mean "friend" or "companion." This name appears in the Greek Old Testament translated as Ῥούθ in Greek.
G4503.emploi: Ruth appears only once in the New Testament, in Matthew 1:5, in the genealogy of Jesus. She is mentioned there as the wife of Boaz and mother of Obed, an essential link in the genealogical chain leading to David and Jesus. She is a remarkable figure in the New Testament, as she is one of the few women named in the genealogy of Jesus, testifying to the importance of her role in God's plan.
G4503.portee: Ruth embodies faithfulness, loyalty, and trust in God in the face of trials. Her story shows that God welcomes those who turn to Him sincerely, even from a foreign nation. It reminds the reader that God can transform situations of distress into blessing and include outsiders in His people and His promises.

sens: Man known in the early Church, son of Simon of Cyrene
G4504G.detail: Rufus is mentioned as one of the two sons of Simon of Cyrene, the man whom the Roman soldiers compelled to carry the cross of Jesus to Calvary (Mark 15:21). The fact that Mark explicitly names him, along with his brother Alexander, suggests that he was known to the readers of the Gospel, likely as an active believer in the Christian community. The Apostle Paul also sends greetings to "Rufus" in his letter to the Romans (Romans 16:13), where he describes him as "chosen in the Lord," indicating that this is the same man and that he had become a prominent disciple.
G4504G.origine: The name Rufus comes from the Latin "rufus," meaning "red-haired." It was a common name in the Roman world of the time. His appearance in two passages of the New Testament (Mark and Romans) shows that this man, son of a Cyrenian, made an impression on the early Christians to the point that he was remembered and greeted in writing.
G4504G.emploi: Rufus appears twice in the New Testament. In Mark 15:21, he is presented as the son of Simon of Cyrene, the man requisitioned to carry the cross of Jesus. That Mark mentions their names, along with that of his brother Alexander, reveals their importance in the communities receiving this Gospel. In Romans 16:13, Paul greets "Rufus, chosen in the Lord, and his mother who has also been a mother to me," attesting that Rufus had become a prominent believer and enjoyed apostolic respect.
G4504G.portee: The mention of Rufus reminds us that Jesus relied on ordinary unknowns to accomplish His work of redemption: it is a man encountered by chance who had to carry His cross, and this moment profoundly marked his family. The fact that Rufus later became a believer "chosen in the Lord" shows how the passion of Christ transformed lives — that of Simon and his sons. We also see that in the early Church, believers remained connected by bonds of genuine affection, which Paul expressed through his personal greetings.

sens: Christian disciple, possibly son of Simon of Cyrene
G4504H.detail: Rufus is a Latin name meaning "red-haired." In the New Testament, it refers to a Roman Christian mentioned by Paul, whom he greets as "the chosen one of the Lord" (Romans 16:13), indicating that he was a respected believer. The Gospel of Mark also reports a Rufus, son of Simon of Cyrene (Mark 15:21), the man who carried the cross of Jesus: it may be the same person, later becoming a pillar of the Church, but the Bible does not explicitly affirm this.
G4504H.origine: Rufus is a name of Latin origin, common in the Roman Empire. It derives from the Latin "rufus," which literally means "red" or "of red color," probably referring to hair color. This type of descriptive name was common among Romans and inhabitants of Romanized regions. By giving him this Latin nickname, the Gospel of Mark and the Apostle Paul integrate Rufus into the Greco-Roman world of their time.
G4504H.emploi: Rufus appears twice in the New Testament. Mark 15:21 mentions him as the son of Simon of Cyrene, who was requisitioned to carry the cross of Jesus. Paul greets him in Romans 16:13 as "the chosen one of the Lord" (a term that designates a Christian in good standing in the Church), along with his mother, whom Paul considers as his own, suggesting a deep friendship and hospitality received. It is possible that he is the same man who grew in faith after being present at the Passion.
G4504H.portee: Rufus embodies the humble believer of whom we ultimately know very little, but who made an impression on the Apostle Paul and the life of the Church. His story, if he is indeed the same Rufus as in Mark, shows how God's grace acts silently: present at the cross without fully knowing it, he later becomes a respected servant of Christ. For the reader, Rufus reminds us that every name recorded in the Church is valued in the eyes of God and His apostles.

sens: A narrow way or alley in a city
A passage or public lane where inhabitants circulate
The place where people gather for various public activities
G4505.detail:
1. The word specifically denotes a narrow way, an alley in urban space — the type of street found in small towns or old neighborhoods. In Matthew 6:2, hypocrites stage themselves in the streets to give alms publicly and be noticed.
2. More broadly, it refers to a public passage that structures city life, where inhabitants circulate and gatherings can take place. In Acts 9:11, the street called "the Straight" is a well-known thoroughfare in Damascus; in Acts 12:10, Peter and the angel exit the prison and advance into a street of the city.
3. The street is the natural place where all people converge — rich and poor, able-bodied and infirm. This is why in Luke 14:21, the master asks his servant to bring in the poor, the crippled, the blind, and the lame to invite them to the feast.
G4505.origine: The Greek word ῥύμη comes from a root that initially evokes the idea of force or rush — the charge of a troop in motion. Gradually, in late Greek (notably in Macedonian), it shifted to the concrete meaning of a way, an alley where people crowd. In the Greek Old Testament, it translates the Hebrew רְחֹב (rechov), which also means a public place or street.
G4505.emploi: The word appears four times in the New Testament, always in the sense of street or alley in a city. Matthew and Luke use it to speak of the streets of Jerusalem or another city; Acts uses it to designate specific ways in Damascus and Jerusalem. In all cases, it is a public space, easily identifiable, where people circulate and urban life unfolds. The context is sometimes that of ostentatious charity (Matthew 6:2), sometimes that of an invitation to a meal (Luke 14:21), and sometimes that of geographical location (Acts 9:11; 12:10).
G4505.portee: The street is where social life and charity play out. It reminds the Christian that authentic generosity does not seek the gaze of men — unlike the hypocrites who give alms in the streets to be seen. It is also the place where the Gospel meets the common people, the marginalized who find themselves there, those whom the master asks to invite to the feast.

sens: To pull someone from danger, to put them in safety
To rescue someone from a power that oppresses them
To save from condemnation or divine wrath
To assist, to provide help
G4506.detail:
1. The verb expresses the action of pulling someone out of immediate peril, like pulling a person from water or from the grasp of an enemy. It is to save someone by placing them in a safe place. Example: "The Lord delivered me from all" the persecutions that Paul suffered (2 Timothy 3:11).
2. The word also refers to being pulled from prolonged domination or oppression — being extracted from the hand of an adversary who holds us captive. Example: "Delivered from the hand of our enemies," the disciples of John the Baptist could "serve Him without fear" (Luke 1:74).
3. Spiritually, to deliver means to save from condemnation or the coming wrath. Jesus delivers us "from the wrath to come" (1 Thessalonians 1:10), and He rescues us from the "power of darkness" (Colossians 1:13).
4. In the Lord's Prayer, deliver expresses divine help against evil: "Deliver us from the evil one" (Matthew 6:13). It is asking God for active protection and immediate assistance.
G4506.origine: The Greek verb ῥύομαι comes from a root that literally means "to pull to oneself, to attract." This image of physical pulling or rescue has extended to spiritual help. In Hebrew, this verb often translates נָצַל (natzal), which also carries the idea of pulling out or saving, as well as גָּאַל (gaal), which evokes deliverance and redemption. The Greek word retains this concrete warmth: one does not deliver abstractly; one pulls the other toward oneself, away from evil.
G4506.emploi: The verb ῥύομαι appears 16 times in the New Testament, mainly in Paul’s writings and in the epistles. It is primarily used with complements that indicate the source of danger: one is delivered "from the evil one" (Matthew 6:13), "from wrath" (1 Thessalonians 1:10), "from the power of darkness" (Colossians 1:13), or "from a threatening death" (2 Corinthians 1:10). Paul uses it to testify to apostolic protection: the Lord delivered him from persecutions (2 Timothy 3:11 and 4:17). Romans 11:26 uses the participle "the Deliverer" to refer to the Messiah who comes from Zion. The word is also used in the passive voice to express our dependence: we are the recipients of a deliverance, not its actors.
G4506.portee: This verb reminds the Christian that their security is not the result of their efforts, but a gift from the Lord. Praying "deliver us from the evil one" is not an abstract formula, but a concrete request: God does not leave us at the mercy of evil. For the persecuted or tested Church, this word affirms that God pulls His own out of peril and that His deliverance is real, historical, and promised even from the coming wrath.

sens: Dirt, filth, that which makes one materially impure
Moral impurity, guilt of sin, that which defiles the soul
G4507.detail:
1. Literally, defilement refers to dirt or filth (that which is ῥυπαρός, soiled, disgusting). The image is of something repugnant that sticks to the skin.
2. Figuratively, it is everything that morally corrupts the soul: sin, malice, everything that makes us "impure" before God. In James 1:21, the apostle invites us to reject "defilement" (that is, bad thoughts, malicious intentions) so that the implanted word in us may grow and save us. Defilement is what obstructs the soul, preventing it from receiving and keeping the Word.
G4507.origine: The word comes from the adjective ῥυπαρός (soiled, dirty) which literally describes what is impure or filthy. The root evokes the image of an accumulation of dirt. In biblical Greek usage, this term first applies to the physical body, then extends to the soul as a spiritual contamination.
G4507.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in James 1:21, where it refers to the moral and spiritual impurity that the believer must reject. James uses it in a context of exhortation to sanctification: for the Word to work in us and save us, we must rid ourselves of everything that morally defiles us. It is a call to integrity of heart and soul.
G4507.portee: This word challenges the Christian about the necessity of inner purity. Rejecting defilement is not just a matter of external behavior: it is cleaning one’s heart of corrupt thoughts, grudges, malice, so that the Word of God can truly take root and transform our lives. It is an invitation to spiritual honesty and growth in Christ.

sens: Dressed in a miserable way, worn and torn
Morally impure, stained by sin
G4508.detail:
1. The word first describes clothing that has lost all dignity: old, torn, dirty, those worn by a poor person. James 2:2 uses it to contrast with "fine clothing" worn by a rich person: it is the "miserably" dressed garment, which reveals nothing of poverty. The image evokes physical dirt, the wear of time.
2. Applied to the soul rather than to clothes, the word becomes moral. Revelation 22:11 speaks of one who is "soiled" and continues to soil himself: it is no longer the dust of the road, but the sin that stains the inner being, the image of spiritual impurity, like a garment that is never washed and becomes repugnant.
G4508.origine: The word comes from the Greek root rhypos, which means dirt, filth. It is the concrete word for saying "unclean." It first describes a physical state: soiled clothes, unwashed body. As often in biblical Greek, the image of the outside (the worn robe) serves to say something about the inside (the corrupted heart).
G4508.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, but in very different contexts. In James 2:2, it qualifies the clothing of the poor person who enters the assembly: it is a critique of favoritism — one looks at external appearance instead of equality before God. In Revelation 22:11, the same word becomes moral and eschatological: it describes the final state of one who hardens in evil, who refuses the salvation offered by Christ. The transition from the physical to the spiritual enriches the meaning: what was a humble metaphor in James becomes a terrible condemnation in Revelation.
G4508.portee: This word reminds the Christian of two truths: that they should never despise the poor because of their worn clothes — true beauty is within — and that persistent sin leaves a deep stain on the soul, a defilement that only Christ can cleanse us from (Revelation 1:5). It is a call both to justice towards the needy and to vigilance against the hardening of the heart.

sens: physical dirt, grime
that which makes impure, that which morally or spiritually defiles
the impurity of a conscience burdened with guilt
G4509.detail: 1. The word primarily denotes concrete dirt, grime that soils the body — the idea of a repugnant substance. 2. It extends to anything that makes someone or something impure and unworthy, particularly in a moral and religious sense: sin, guilt, anything that distances us from God (1 Peter 3:21 speaks of the "stains" of the body, but by extension of all forms of impurity). 3. In the context of baptism (1 Peter 3:21), the word particularly evokes the conscience burdened with guilt — the traces of sin etched in the soul — from which the believer purifies themselves through their commitment to God.
G4509.origine: The word comes from a Greek root meaning "to be dirty" or "to be defiled." It expresses the concrete image of physical dirt, then rises to moral and spiritual meaning. In Hebrew, the Old Testament uses words like צוֹאָה ("filth, grime") and טָמֵא ("to be unclean") in the same religious context.
G4509.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Peter 3:21, where Peter explains the meaning of baptism. He contrasts the external cleansing of the body with the internal purification of the conscience: baptism is not a mere rite that washes away material stains, but an act by which the believer solemnly commits to God and receives salvation. This context shows that "stain" encompasses all forms of impurity — physical, moral, spiritual — from which the believer must be freed.
G4509.portee: This word reminds the believer that salvation is not an external or superficial purification, but a deep internal transformation. Baptism signifies that we acknowledge our guilt before God and commit to live for Him, relying on the resurrection of Jesus. It is an invitation to take seriously the gravity of sin and the reality of forgiveness offered in Christ.

sens: to make impure or dirty
to morally stain
to remain in a state of defilement
G4510.detail:
1. To make something impure or covered with dirt — this is the concrete image of the word. The verb comes from the root "rhypos" which literally denotes dirt, grime (Revelation 22:11).
2. To morally or spiritually stain a person, to corrupt, to contaminate them through sin — the image shifts from the physical to the moral. This is a frequent sense in the Greek Old Testament.
3. To persist voluntarily in a state of moral defilement, to refuse to purify oneself — the emphasis is on the continuity and deliberate rejection of purity (Revelation 22:11, where the one who is defiled continues to defile themselves).
G4510.origine: The verb comes from the noun "rhypos" (dirt, grime) and is constructed as a simple verb in Greek (-ōō). This root first evokes the very concrete image of physical grime; the verb extends it to the moral domain of corruption and sin. The Greek translators of the Old Testament used this word to translate the Hebrew notions of ritual or moral impurity.
G4510.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Revelation 22:11. John places it in his final vision: as time comes to an end and everyone receives their final fate, the one who remains unjust remains so, the one who is defiled continues to defile themselves. The context emphasizes the irrevocability of judgment — at this ultimate stage, the sinner can no longer change direction and sinks further into their own defilement.
G4510.portee: This word reminds us that sin is not a mere accident or a temporary stain: it is a defilement that worsens as long as one refuses to clean it. For the believer, it invites them to seek purification through Christ right now, for each refusal to repent further entraps us. It is a warning against the gradual hardening of the heart.

sens: Flow of blood outside the body, involuntary and prolonged bleeding
Hemorrhage that weakens and renders impure according to the law of Moses
G4511.detail: 1. The word denotes the continuous and pathological flow of blood. The woman in Mark 5:25 and Luke 8:43 suffered from it for twelve years: it was not a single wound, but a chronic bleeding that drained her body and her finances (she had consulted all the doctors without success). In Luke 8:44, this flow suddenly stops upon contact with Jesus' garment. 2. According to the Law, such a loss rendered the woman ritually unclean (Leviticus 15): she could not enter the temple or approach others without contaminating them. This is why she "came up behind" (Luke 8:44) — she did not dare to show herself. Her healing is thus also a social and spiritual restoration.
G4511.origine: The word comes from the Greek root ἔρρω ("to flow"), which describes any flow or discharge. In Hebrew from the Old Testament, the word זוֹב (zob) is found, which has the same meaning: an abnormal discharge from the body, declaring impure the one who suffers from it. The Greek of the New Testament borrows this notion to describe the illness of this woman with medical precision.
G4511.emploi: This word appears only three times in the New Testament, all in the account of the healing of the woman with the hemorrhage (Mark 5:25, Luke 8:43-44). Matthew recounts the same story (9:20-22) but does not use this specific term. The context is always one of prolonged suffering, legal impurity, and miraculous healing. Luke's two uses specify the long-standing nature of the ailment ("for twelve years") and its devastating effect (financial ruin, absence of healing). The third use marks the moment of deliverance: "the hemorrhage stopped."
G4511.portee: This healing account speaks to the heart of those suffering from a chronic illness or feeling excluded. The woman had tried everything, lost everything, but simple faith in Jesus restored her — both physically and socially. For the Christian reader, it is a sign that Jesus is not ashamed of illness or impurity: He touches and purifies her. It is also a call to discreet yet bold faith: she did not ask for permission, she simply dared to touch Him.

sens: Fold or crease in the skin of the face, mark of aging
Defect or mark of dirt on a surface
G4512.detail:
1. A wrinkle is a fold that creases the skin, particularly on the face: it is the visible sign of the passage of time and the aging of the body. In Ephesians 5:27, the Apostle Paul speaks of the Church without wrinkle, an image of intact, youthful, and unblemished beauty.
2. Figuratively, a wrinkle more broadly denotes any defect or mark that tarnishes appearance: a trace of dirt, an imperfection. This is why Paul contrasts the Church without wrinkle to one that would be disfigured, to express the purity and perfection it must testify to.
G4512.origine: The Greek word rhutis denotes the fold or wrinkle that marks the skin — it is a concrete, very visual term. It comes from a root that evokes the idea of crumpling or wrinkling. The Latin ruga, very close, confirms this universal image: in all civilizations, wrinkles are witnesses of time. The word appears only once in the New Testament.
G4512.emploi: Rhutis appears only once in the Bible: in Ephesians 5:27. Paul uses it to describe the Church as it will appear one day before Christ — not as it is now, still marked by flaws and wounds, but glorified and restored. The wrinkle symbolizes here all visible defects, any imperfection that would diminish the beauty of the Church. It is a poetic and evocative image: just as a smooth and youthful face inspires beauty and health, a Church without wrinkle will be the perfect reflection of Christ's holiness.
G4512.portee: This word invites the Christian to contemplate what the Church is called to become: not a perfect community right now, but destined for complete transformation, purified and glorified in the presence of Christ. It also encourages not to focus on external appearances, but on inner purity and the work of sanctification that the Holy Spirit accomplishes in each one.

sens: belonging to Rome or the Roman Empire
spoken or written in Latin
characteristic of Roman culture
G4513.detail:
1. This word qualifies what belongs to Rome, the powerful city and empire that dominates the Mediterranean world at the time of Jesus. In Luke 23:38, the inscription on the cross is written "in Greek, Latin, and Hebrew letters": "Latin" translates this adjective, designating the official language of Rome and its administration.

2. By extension, it describes anything related to the Latin language, the mother tongue of the Romans and vehicle of imperial power. Latin was the administrative and military language of the Empire.

3. It also characterizes anything that bears the imprint of Roman civilization — its customs, laws, institutions, and dominant way of life.
G4513.origine: This Greek word derives directly from the name of Rome (Rhômê) and literally means "that which concerns Rome." It is formed on the model of usual Greek adjectives. The Greeks, in contact with the growing Roman power, needed words to designate what was specific to this conquering people. Latin, the language of the Romans, gradually became a language of power in the Greco-Roman world.
G4513.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 23:38, where it refers to the inscription placed above the crucified Jesus. Luke specifies that this inscription was written in three languages: "Greek, Latin, and Hebrew." The choice of the word "Roman" here is not accidental: Luke emphasizes that even at the time of the crucifixion, Roman authority asserts its power by imposing its official language alongside Greek and Hebrew. This detail highlights the political and cultural context of the Passion.
G4513.portee: This discreet mention of the Roman text on the cross reminds readers that Jesus was condemned by a foreign power, Rome, and not solely by the Jewish authorities. It evokes the humiliation of a Jewish king executed by Roman methods, but also the irony of the message displayed: even the Romans, through this inscription in multiple languages, announced to all peoples that Jesus was "the King of the Jews."

sens: inhabitant or citizen of Rome or the Roman Empire
person enjoying the rights of Roman citizenship with its legal privileges
G4514.detail:
1. The word primarily designates one who belongs to Rome and its empire, whether a resident of the capital or a subject of Rome dispersed in the provinces. When the Jewish leaders fear that Jesus may gain too much influence, they say: "The Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation" (John 11:48) — referring to the Roman authorities governing Judea.
2. More specifically, "Roman" designates one who possesses the legal status of Roman citizenship, accompanied by rights and immunities. Paul, although a Jew born in Tarsus, invokes this privilege to escape illegal punishments: "we are Romans" (Acts 16:37), he refuses a public flogging without trial. The Roman tribune himself recognizes him with fear: "This man is a Roman" (Acts 22:26).
G4514.origine: The Greek word Rhōmaios comes directly from the name of the city of Rome (Rhōmē). It is the ordinary gentilic term used to designate anything related to Rome. In contemporary texts, it applies both to the inhabitants of the city and to all citizens of the empire who enjoyed the rights of Roman citizenship, a highly coveted and jealously guarded status.
G4514.emploi: The word appears twelve times in the New Testament, almost exclusively in Acts (12 occurrences) and only once in John. It is used in contexts of political or legal confrontation: the Jews fear Roman military intervention (John 11:48), the magistrates of Philippi fear reprisals upon discovering that they have mistreated Roman citizens (Acts 16:37-38), and Paul himself brandishes his status as a Roman citizen to protect himself from beatings or arbitrary imprisonment (Acts 22:25-27). The word always conveys the idea of institutional power and legal protection: to be Roman is to benefit from guarantees that others do not possess.
G4514.portee: For the Christian reader, this entry reminds us that the Gospel spreads in a world of empires and human powers. Paul, as a Roman citizen, seeks justice according to Roman laws themselves — a lesson in prudence and civic responsibility. But the irony is that his earthly citizenship, however prestigious, is nothing compared to the far higher title of citizen of the kingdom of God. The contrast invites the believer to seek a city whose builder is God, not a human empire.

sens: in the Latin language
in the Latin manner of expression
G4515.detail:
1. In the Latin language: the word designates the use of the Latin language, that of Rome and the Roman Empire. In John 19:20, the inscription placed above the crucified Jesus was written in three languages — Hebrew, Greek, and Latin — so that all could read it: Latin was the official language of the Roman power occupying Judea.
2. More broadly, it also means "in the Roman manner" or "according to Roman usage": it marks belonging to Rome, its empire, and its culture.
G4515.origine: The word comes from Rhômê (Ρώμη), which means Rome, the capital of the empire. The suffix -isti indicates the language or manner of speaking specific to a people or empire, as one says "in Greek" (hellênisti) or "in Hebrew." It is an adverb formed from the adjective Roman to express the use of a language or a manner.
G4515.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in John 19:20. It refers to one of the three languages in which Pilate had the title of condemnation inscribed above the cross. This presence of Latin underscores Roman authority over occupied Judea: even at the moment of Jesus' execution, Rome imposes its language alongside Hebrew (the religious and national language of the Jews) and Greek (the common language of commerce and Mediterranean culture).
G4515.portee: This word reminds us that Jesus died under Roman authority, the occupier. The trilingual inscription symbolizes the three worlds that meet at the cross: the Jewish world, the Greek world, and the Roman world. It is also a sign that the Gospel, born in Jewish land, is destined to extend to all peoples and cultures.

sens: Capital of the Roman Empire, seat of the political and military power of the empire
Major commercial and administrative center of the ancient West
Symbolic place of the expansion of the Christian faith into the heart of the pagan world
G4516.detail:
1. Rome is the great capital city of the Roman Empire, from where decisions governing the known world are made. It is here that Claudius, the emperor, gives the order that expels the Jews, as noted in Acts 18:2. Paul dreams of going there, not out of tourist curiosity, but because it is the heart of power: he had the plan to go to Rome, as he said in Acts 19:21.
2. For Paul, Rome symbolizes the center of the mission: after witnessing in Jerusalem and the Greek regions, he must absolutely testify in Rome as well, for it is the nerve center of the ancient world (Acts 23:11). The Lord Himself confirms this plan as a necessary step in His work.
3. In Acts 28:14-16, Paul finally reaches Rome as a prisoner, but as a messenger of Christ: he particularly stays with a soldier who guards him, which allows him to live and preach. The presence of a Christian community in Rome (Romans 1:7) shows that the Gospel has already penetrated the heart of the pagan world.
G4516.origine: Rome comes from Latin and is the same in the Greek of the New Testament. The proper name of the city has remained unchanged in all texts, as it is a name of universal empire. In the Greek Old Testament, Rome is not found because this power was not yet dominant; it emerges as a major power after Macedonia, which explains why the New Testament speaks of it abundantly.
G4516.emploi: Rome appears 8 times in the Greek New Testament, all occurrences found in Paul's epistles and in Acts. It is first mentioned in Acts 18:2 due to Claudius' decree; then Paul makes it a central project of his mission (Acts 19:21), which the Lord approves (Acts 23:11). The last three chapters of Acts recount Paul's journey to Rome in chains (Acts 28:14-16). The Epistle to the Romans, addressed to the believers in Rome, shows that a church has formed there. Paul sees Rome not as an ordinary city, but as the pinnacle of his testimony for Christ.
G4516.portee: Rome represents for every Christian the necessity of bringing the Gospel even to the highest and most difficult places in the world. Paul was not afraid to go to Rome in chains, for he knew that the Lord would send him there. It is a reminder that the Christian faith is not confined to synagogues or Greek regions, but must reach the centers of earthly power. Rome also symbolizes how, through his presence and testimony, Paul established a church in the very heart of the empire that seemed indomitable.

sens: To have strength, physical or moral vigor
Goodbye, farewell (wish for strength and health)
G4517.detail:
1. The verb ῥώννυμι primarily means "to be strong" or "to have strength" — it conveys the idea of vigor, robustness, whether physical or moral. It evokes the capacity to hold firm, to resist.
2. However, in practice, in the New Testament, it is mostly encountered in the past imperative form, as "ἔρρωσο" or "ἔρρωσθε", as a farewell formula: it is a "goodbye" or "farewell". This expression wishes the one departing to be strong, to remain vigorous — hence its meaning of "be strong, take care of yourself". It can be seen in official letters or decrees of the time.
G4517.origine: The word comes from a root that expresses strength and vigor. The form "ἔρρωμαι" found in the texts is a perfect tense, indicating an acquired and stable state: "I have become strong and I remain so." It is from this nuance that the usage as a polite formula arises: one wishes someone to remain in this state of strength.
G4517.emploi: This verb appears only twice in the Greek New Testament we possess, both in the Epistle to the Acts, and always in this passive and fixed form. In Acts 15:29, it is the decree from Jerusalem addressed to mixed churches: the official letter ends with "ἔρρωσθε", a farewell to the communities. In Acts 23:30, it is the letter from the tribune Lysias to Governor Felix that ends similarly. These two occurrences show that the word has become a conventional formula in administrative and solemn correspondences of the time — the equivalent of "be vigorous" or "goodbye" found in the papyrus documents of the era.
G4517.portee: This word shows us how the early Church communicated officially with its members, and how the Roman and Jewish authorities of the time greeted each other. It is a concrete detail that anchors the narrative of Acts in real history and allows us to touch the texture of Christian life in the first century. The wish for "strength" also reveals a faith: in a hostile world, the Church wishes its members not comfort, but spiritual robustness.

sens: You have left me alone, without help
You have turned away from me
You have delivered me to suffering
G4518.detail:
1. The word expresses the action of leaving someone alone, without help or protection. It is the cry of Jesus on the cross: "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" (Matthew 27:46). The image is one of total abandonment, as if God had withdrawn.
2. Beyond mere physical abandonment, the word denotes a turning away: God turns His face, His attention, His support away. It is the feeling of being rejected, of having lost the support one expected from the Father.
3. In the context of the Passion, abandonment takes the form of being delivered to death and suffering. Jesus expresses not an accusation, but an anguished question: why this separation at this supreme hour?
G4518.origine: This Aramaic word (the mother tongue of Jesus) comes from the root שְׁבַק (shbaq), which means "to leave, abandon, release". It translates the Hebrew עָזַב (azab), whose primary image is that of rejection or abandonment. This root often expresses in the Old Testament the idea that God abandons His people or that the people abandon Him, but here it is placed in the mouth of the dying Son of God.
G4518.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both in the account of the Passion: Matthew 27:46 and Mark 15:34. Both evangelists report the same cry, in Aramaic. Jesus quotes Psalm 22:2, where the psalmist also cries, "My God, why have you forsaken me?" This cry is not an expression of final despair, but an entry into the reality of substitution: by taking our sins, Jesus experiences the separation that sin produces with God. It is the moment when He bears the weight of our condemnation.
G4518.portee: This cry reveals the depth of Jesus' sacrifice: it is not only about physical suffering, but about the experience of divine judgment against sin. For the believer, this terrible moment also speaks the truth of redemption: Jesus bore alone what we deserved, so that we would never know this abandonment. That is why we can cry out, even in suffering, that God never abandons us.

sens: The military troops, the fighting forces of a kingdom
The entirety of celestial and divine powers, the angels and spiritual beings
The totality of God's forces, which makes Him all-powerful
G4519.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to armies in the military sense, that is, the organized troops of a kingdom or nation. This is the concrete and historical meaning of the Hebrew word from which it is derived.
2. It extends to the heavenly army: the angels and spirits that form the court and armies of heaven, under God's sovereignty. This is suggested by the expression "Lord of hosts" in the prophecies.
3. The title "Lord of hosts" (Sabaoth in Hebrew) becomes a divine name that emphasizes God's power: it is the Lord who commands all forces, both visible and invisible, earthly and heavenly. This evokes His absolute sovereignty and limitless authority (Romans 9:29; James 5:4).
G4519.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew verb צבא (tsaba) which means to fight, to wage war. The noun צָבָא (tsaba) thus designates an army, a troop organized for war. In the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament), this word is transcribed in Greek as "Sabaoth." The complete expression "Lord of hosts" (צְבָאוֹת יְהוָה in Hebrew) uses the plural of the word, highlighting the multiplicity of forces under divine command: both earthly armies and celestial powers. This expression becomes a major title for God in the prophets, particularly in Isaiah.
G4519.emploi: The word "Sabaoth" appears only twice in the Greek New Testament, and only in the epistles of Paul and James, each time in the citation or allusion to the phrase from Isaiah: "Lord of hosts." In Romans 9:29, Paul quotes Isaiah 1:9 to affirm that God, who commands the heavenly and earthly armies, has reserved a remnant of Israel. In James 5:4, the apostle invokes the same title to affirm that the cry of the workers wronged reaches the ears of the Almighty Lord, who sees and judges. The word thus remains a rare but powerful theological term that evokes divine majesty and God's omniscience.
G4519.portee: This title reveals God's absolute power and sovereignty: He is not an isolated monarch, but the Lord who commands all the forces of the universe. For the believer, this means that God is never powerless in the face of injustices or threats: He sees all, He commands all. It is an invitation to trust: the God we serve is the Lord of hosts, far more powerful than anything that could oppose us.

sens: A day of rest dedicated to God, according to Jewish law
A state of rest and peace in the believer's life
The spiritual fulfillment of the rest announced in the Old Testament
G4520.detail:
1. Literally, it is the action of keeping the Sabbath, this day of rest that Jewish law requires: no work, a consecration to God. It is the Sabbath as observance, as seen from Exodus (Exodus 16:30).
2. But in the Epistle to the Hebrews, the word signifies much more: a deep and lasting spiritual rest that God promises to His people in faith in Christ (Hebrews 4:9). It is not just a day that comes every week; it is the entrance into a permanent peace.
3. It is the idea that the rest of the seventh day was a figure, a shadow of the eternal rest that believers receive by entering into the completed work of Christ. The true Sabbath is ceasing to rely on oneself and resting in God.
G4520.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb "sabbatizo" (to keep the Sabbath), which itself goes back to the Hebrew word "shabbat" (rest, cessation). The root means to stop, to cease work. In the language of Hellenistic Jews, this term expresses Jewish religious observance while opening, in the Epistles, to a deeper spiritual reality: the rest that God Himself knows and shares with His children.
G4520.emploi: The word appears only once in Hebrews 4:9, but it summarizes a central teaching of this epistle. The author recalls that after creation, God rested on the seventh day (Genesis 2:2-3), and that this rest remains accessible "for the people of God." This rest is not physical inactivity, but the trusting abandonment of our own efforts, the acceptance that Christ has completed the work of salvation. It is a rest that begins now for the believer and will be fully realized in eternity.
G4520.portee: This word frees the believer from the anxiety of having to "save himself" through his works or merits. It invites him to enter, starting today, into God's rest — not inactivity, but the quiet confidence that everything is accomplished in Christ. It is an invitation to stop struggling alone and to trust, each day, in Him who said: "Come to me, all you who are weary" (Matthew 11:28).

sens: The seventh day of the week, a day of rest dedicated to God according to the Law of Moses
Any day, a particular day
A whole week, a period of seven days
G4521.detail:
1. The Sabbath is the seventh day of the week, the day when Jews cease all work to honor God and rest. It is a fundamental commandment of the Law: God rested on the seventh day after creation, and Israel must imitate Him. In Jesus' time, the Pharisees strictly interpreted this prohibition: one cannot pluck ears of grain on the Sabbath (Matthew 12:1), nor heal a sick person (Luke 13:14), nor wash (John 9:14). Jesus, however, disrupts these practices by healing the infirm on that day, which provokes the anger of the religious leaders (John 5:16).
2. By extension, "Sabbath" simply designates a day, a particular day: when Mark says "a Sabbath day" (Mark 2:23) or when referring to the first day of the week after the Sabbath (Mark 16:9), the word serves to situate a moment in the calendar.
3. Rarely, the word designates a whole week, a period of seven days: Paul recommends setting aside money "on the first day of the week" (1 Corinthians 16:2), where "week" translates the Greek sabbaton in the sense of an interval of seven days.
G4521.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew and Aramaic shabbat (שַׁבָּת), which means "rest." In Greek, it is written sabbaton or sabbata (the latter may have been taken for a plural, which led to the creation of the singular sabbaton). The Mosaic Law establishes the Sabbath as a day of complete cessation from work, a sign of the covenant between God and Israel. This commandment goes back to Exodus 20:8 and is one of the Ten Commandments.
G4521.emploi: The word appears 62 times in the New Testament, mostly in the Gospels and Acts. It primarily designates the weekly day of rest that Jews observe. The Gospels report many conflicts: Jesus heals the sick on the Sabbath (Luke 6:7, John 5:9), which the Pharisees judge illegal; He defends His disciples who pluck ears of grain (Mark 2:23-28); He teaches in the synagogue on that day (Luke 4:16). Acts shows that the early Christians, all Jews, continue to gather in the synagogue on the Sabbath (Acts 13:14, 16:13), while also holding assemblies on the first day of the week (Acts 20:7). Paul asserts that the Sabbath is no longer an obligation for believers in Christ (Colossians 2:16).
G4521.portee: The Sabbath reveals a central tension of the New Testament: between the old Law and the new freedom in Christ. For Jews, it is a sign of the rest promised by God and of His love for His people. For Jesus and the early Church, strict observance is not essential — what matters is doing good and honoring God with all one's heart. The Christian today is not bound to the weekly Sabbath, but the principle remains: God calls each one to rest, to trust, and to prioritize Him in their lives.

sens: Large fishing net that is dragged through the water
Figuratively, that which captures or ensnares
G4522.detail:
1. A large fishing net, specifically designed to be thrown or dragged through the water to catch fish. It is a common working tool in Galilee during the time of Jesus, where fishing supported the local economy. In the parable of Matthew 13:47, Jesus compares the kingdom of heaven to such a net thrown into the sea that gathers fish of every kind — some good, others bad — which will be sorted at the end of time.
2. The image of the net is also used to denote that which captures or ensnares, particularly in a spiritual sense: the net can represent a trap, a snare, or a device that attracts and holds. This figurative dimension is less developed in the New Testament for this specific word, but it is present in the biblical logic of fishing as a symbol of capture.
G4522.origine: The Greek word sagēnē comes from a root meaning "to drag" or "to draw along." It is a technical term borrowed from the vocabulary of fishermen. In the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint), it primarily translates the Hebrew term herem, which designates various types of nets and traps. The family of fishing words in Greek also includes other terms like amphiblestron (circular net) and diktyon (general net), with which sagēnē shares the same concrete realm of capture.
G4522.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament: in Matthew 13:47, in the parable of the net. Jesus describes the kingdom of heaven as similar to a net thrown into the sea that gathers fish of every kind — some good to keep, others to throw away. This parable extends the teaching on the presence of good and evil in the kingdom until the final judgment. The unique and parabolic use of the word shows that Jesus is addressing listeners familiar with this fishing profession, particularly in Galilee.
G4522.portee: This parable of the net teaches that the kingdom of God now welcomes all who believe, without apparent distinction: righteous and unrighteous, wise and foolish. But it also reminds that this mixture is only temporary: at the end of time, a sorting will take place, and only the good will be kept. For the Christian, this image of the net invites vigilance: no complacency in the face of evil present in the Church, and trust that God will accomplish judgment in His time.

sens: Member of a Jewish religious sect during the time of Jesus
Man attached to the written law and hostile to oral traditions
Who denies the resurrection of the dead and the existence of angels
G4523.detail:
1. The Sadducees form a sect or religious group among the Jews during the time of Jesus, mentioned in Matthew 3:7, Mark 12:18, Luke 20:27. They are sometimes opposed to the Pharisees, as in Matthew 16:1 where both groups come together to question Jesus.
2. They are characterized by their strict adherence to the written Law of Moses and their rejection of the oral traditions that the Pharisees uphold. In Matthew 22:23-34, they ask Jesus questions about the resurrection, showing their fundamental theological disagreement with other Jewish groups.
3. The Sadducees denied the resurrection of the dead, angels, and spirits: in Acts 23:6-8, Paul provokes a dispute between Pharisees and Sadducees by mentioning the resurrection, revealing their complete opposition on this point. They primarily represented the aristocracy and the clergy of the Temple, unlike the Pharisees who had more popular influence.
G4523.origine: The word comes from צָדוֹק (Tsadoq in Hebrew), the name of the high priest during the time of King David (2 Kings 15:24). The Sadducees claimed descent from this ancient priestly lineage. The Greek name Σαδδουκαῖος is a simple transliteration, retaining the Hebrew form to designate the religious group stemming from this heritage.
G4523.emploi: The word appears 14 times in the New Testament, exclusively in the four Gospels and Acts. Matthew mentions them most often (7 times), notably in 3:7 where John the Baptist calls them to repentance, and in 16:1-12 where Jesus warns His disciples against "the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees." In the other three Gospels, the Sadducees mainly appear during doctrinal controversies: Mark 12:18 and Luke 20:27 report their question about the resurrection, and Acts 4:1, 5:17, 23:6-8 show their opposition to the early Church, particularly to the preaching of the resurrection of Jesus.
G4523.portee: Understanding who the Sadducees are helps the reader grasp the religious tensions of Judaism during the time of Jesus and why His preaching of the resurrection particularly offends this group. It also shows how the early Church faced serious doctrinal objections: the resurrection of Jesus was a scandal for those who denied the resurrection itself. Finally, this group illustrates the danger of a religious authority separated from the people and closed to spiritual truths beyond the written letter.

sens: Ancestor of Jesus according to Matthew's genealogy
G4524.detail: Zadok is a name that appears in the genealogy of Jesus Christ as reported by Matthew. He is the son of Azor and the father of Achim, placing him somewhere in the long chain of Jesus' ancestors between the Exile and the birth of the Messiah.
G4524.origine: The name Zadok (Hebrew צָדוֹק, Tsadoq) means "just" or "one who is just," from the Hebrew verb צדק (tsedaq) which means "to be just." It is a name borne by several important figures in the Old Testament, notably by the high priest Zadok under David and Solomon. Matthew includes this name in his genealogy to show the continuity between Israel's ancient history and its fulfillment in Jesus.
G4524.emploi: Zadok appears only once in the New Testament, in Matthew 1:14, in the genealogy of Jesus. Matthew lists no fewer than forty-two generations from Abraham to Jesus, and Zadok is among the ancestors situated after the Babylonian Exile. His brief appearance in this context shows that Matthew seeks to establish an authentic legal and historical lineage for Jesus, demonstrating His right to be recognized as the son of David and king of Israel.
G4524.portee: The presence of Zadok in this genealogy reminds readers that Jesus is part of the real history of God's people. It attests that the promised Messiah is not a mythical figure, but a man with a true genealogy, real roots in the people of Israel. This inscription of Jesus in a human chain, far from diminishing His greatness, shows how God has fulfilled His promises in the concrete history of men.

sens: Proprement, pour un chien, agiter la queue, caresser
Au figuré, chercher à séduire ou tromper quelqu'un par de belles paroles
Être secoué, troublé, ébranlé dans sa conviction
G4525.detail: 1. The word first paints the image of a dog wagging its tail to caress or to be seen favorably: a tender gesture that often hides a calculated intention. 2. Figuratively, it denotes the action of flattering someone, seducing, or deceiving them with sweet and flattering words — the idea is that one 'shakes' them emotionally to divert them from their path. 3. In the passive form (as in 1 Thessalonians 3:3), the word means to be troubled, shaken in one's faith or convictions: 'so that no one would be shaken by these present tribulations' — that is, not to waver or be shaken by suffering.
G4525.origine: The word comes from the concrete image of a wavering movement: to shake, to stir. In Greek, it is related to words that express swaying or flexibility. The primary image is that of a dog wagging its tail to ingratiate itself; from there, the figurative sense of seducing or troubling has developed.
G4525.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Thessalonians 3:3, in the passive form. Paul uses it to exhort the believers in Thessalonica not to be troubled or shaken by the persecutions they are enduring. The apostle means: do not be shaken in your faith or diverted from your conviction by present sufferings. It is a call to steadfastness and perseverance.
G4525.portee: This word reminds the reader that authentic faith should not be shaken by trials, temptations, or flattering words. The image of the dog wagging its tail also warns us that sweet words can hide a deceptive intention: it urges us to discern between true exhortation and seduction. For the Christian, it is a call to remain firm in one's convictions, regardless of the circumstances.

sens: Tissu grossier tressé, généralement en poils d'animal, de couleur sombre
Sac ou conteneur confectionné dans ce tissu
Vêtement porté pour exprimer le deuil ou la pénitence
G4526.detail:
1. The sack is a rough and rustic fabric made from camel or goat hair, hence its prickly and uncomfortable texture. In Revelation 6:12, the text describes the sun turning black 'like a sackcloth', emphasizing the dark and dull color of the fabric.
2. This fabric was used to make containers or sacks intended to transport and store goods, particularly provisions. This is the common usage of the word in daily life.
3. Worn as clothing, the sack became a powerful symbol: the one who donned it expressed through this uncomfortable and humiliating gesture their grief, repentance, or intercession before God. In Matthew 11:21 and Luke 10:13, Jesus mentions the cities that 'would have repented by wearing sackcloth and ashes' — two signs of affliction combined to show sincere conversion. In Revelation 11:3, the two witnesses prophesy 'clothed in sackcloth', thus displaying their prophetic solemnity and total commitment.
G4526.origine: The Greek word σάκκος comes directly from the Hebrew שַׂק (saq), which shows the borrowing of biblical culture from a well-established Eastern practice. The root first designates the material itself — the coarse weaving — before referring to the object made from it. The Greeks adopted the word as is, without translation, because the fabric was known and characteristic of life in the Near East.
G4526.emploi: The word appears four times in the New Testament, all in serious or solemn contexts. Two uses (Matthew 11:21 and Luke 10:13) are identical: it is the same saying of Jesus, where sackcloth represents the garment of repentance. One use (Revelation 6:12) describes the fabric itself to evoke the blackness of the sky during the sixth seal. The last (Revelation 11:3) shows the two witnesses clothed in sackcloth during their prophecy. The word is never used in a neutral or trivial sense: it always carries a spiritual weight, that of mourning, repentance, or prophetic gravity.
G4526.portee: The sack reminds the reader that true repentance is not a hidden internal matter, but a visible transformation that engages the whole body. It is a call not to separate faith from its outward manifestations: to truly believe is to be ready to publicly humble oneself before God and before men. This raw image remains powerful: it confronts us with the question of what we would truly be willing to suffer and to humble ourselves for.

sens: Ancêtre de Jésus, père de Booz
G4527G.detail: Salmon is a figure from the Old Testament who appears in the genealogy of Jesus as reported by Luke. He is the father of Boaz, who is himself an ancestor of David and thus of Jesus (Luke 3:32). His name appears in the lineage of the kings and ancestors of the Messiah.
G4527G.origine: The name Salmon comes from the Hebrew שֶׁלַח (Shalah), which means 'sent' or 'dart'. It is a traditional Hebrew name borne by several figures in the history of Israel, but the Salmon in the genealogy of Jesus is the one who fathered Boaz.
G4527G.emploi: Salmon appears only once in the genealogy of Jesus according to Luke (Luke 3:32), where he is presented as the son of Nahshon and the father of Boaz. This mention places him in the direct line leading to David and Jesus. In other biblical passages, Salma (or Salmon according to variants) is also mentioned as the founder of Bethlehem.
G4527G.portee: Salmon reminds us that Jesus is rooted in the concrete history of Israel. His ancestors are not mythological figures, but real men belonging to the people of God. This genealogy shows us that Jesus is truly the heir of the promises made to David and to Israel.

sens: fils de Seruch dans la généalogie de Jésus
G4527H.detail: Sala is a figure from the Old Testament who appears in the genealogy of Jesus according to Luke. He is the father of Seruch and the son of Ragau. His name is listed in the long chain of ancestors of Jesus that Luke enumerates, tracing back to Adam to show that Jesus is truly the heir of the promise made to the people of Israel (Luke 3:35).
G4527H.origine: The name Sala comes from the Hebrew שֶׁלַח (Shalah or Shelah). This figure is mentioned in the genealogy of Genesis as a son of Shem, a distant ancestor of Jesus. The Hebrew name suggests the idea of sending or mission, which may evoke God's plan continuing through the generations.
G4527H.emploi: Sala appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 3:35, in the genealogy of Jesus that Luke traces. This genealogy goes back from Jesus to Adam and shows the family ties that connect Jesus to the patriarchs of the Old Testament and to Adam himself. Sala thus represents a link in the chain of those through whom God prepared the arrival of the Messiah.

sens: Ancestor of Jesus in Luke's genealogy
G4528G.detail: Salathiel is a man's name that appears in the genealogy of Jesus reported by the Gospel of Luke. He is presented as the father of Zerubbabel and the son of Neri (Luke 3:27). This name also appears in Matthew, where Salathiel is mentioned as the father of Zerubbabel and son of Jeconiah. In both genealogies, Salathiel connects Jesus to the royal line of Israel, particularly during the period of the Babylonian exile and the return.
G4528G.origine: The name Salathiel comes from the Hebrew שְׁאַלְתִּיאֵל (Shealtiel), which literally means "the one whom God has asked for" or "asked of God." This name expresses the idea that a child was requested from God through the prayers of his parents. It appears in the Old Testament in connection with the return from exile (Ezra 3:2, Nehemiah 12:1), where Salathiel is mentioned as a leader of the people.
G4528G.emploi: Salathiel appears only twice in the New Testament: in Matthew 1:12 and in Luke 3:27, both in the genealogies of Jesus. In Matthew, he is listed in the genealogy of Joseph from the Babylonian exile. In Luke, he is presented in a different genealogy, which explains the variations between the two lists. In both cases, Salathiel is an important link in the genealogical chain that establishes Jesus' connection to the house of David and the kingship of Israel.
G4528G.portee: Salathiel reminds the reader that Jesus is part of the real history of Israel, particularly the crucial period of exile and return. His presence in the genealogy shows that Jesus is the heir of the promises made to David, fulfilling the messianic hope of the Jewish people. It invites us to recognize that the coming of Jesus is not a divine improvisation, but the culmination of a plan of God that spans centuries.

sens: Man who lived after the Babylonian exile
Son of Jeconiah in the genealogy of Jesus
G4528H.detail:
1. Salathiel is a figure who appears in the history of Israel after King Jeconiah and the people were deported to Babylon. He represents a generation of the exile, those who lived in captivity or shortly thereafter.
2. In the genealogy of Jesus according to Matthew, Salathiel is presented as the son of Jeconiah, the king of Judah who was exiled. He fathered Zerubbabel, who would lead the return and the reconstruction of the Temple after the exile (Matthew 1:12). This place in the genealogy shows that Jesus descends from the royal lineage, even through these generations marked by the trial of exile.
G4528H.origine: The name Salathiel comes from the Hebrew שְׁאַלְתִּיאֵל (Sh'altiel), which means "I have asked God" or "God has heard my request." This name reflects the faith of a generation that, during the exile, implored God to remember His people and restore them.
G4528H.emploi: Salathiel appears only once in the Segond, in Matthew 1:12, in the official genealogy of the Messiah. He is also found in Luke 3:27 in another genealogical version. He is an essential link in the chain that connects the promise made to David, through the devastating exile, to Jesus. His appearance emphasizes that even the Babylonian captivity did not interrupt God's plan for His people and for the Messiah.
G4528H.portee: The mention of Salathiel in the genealogy of Jesus reassures the reader: even in the darkest hours — the exile, the destruction of the Temple, the apparent abandonment — God has never forgotten His promises. Jesus descends from those who experienced punishment and restoration, showing that divine faithfulness transcends crises and that hope remains alive even after judgment.

sens: Main port and city of the island of Cyprus
G4529.detail: Salamis was the most important city of Cyprus at the time of the New Testament. It is where Paul and Barnabas landed during their first missionary journey, and they proclaimed the Gospel in the synagogues of the Jews (Acts 13:5).
G4529.origine: Salamis was a well-known ancient city in the Greek world, strategically located on the eastern coast of Cyprus. It was a commercial center and a major port, a natural stopping point for travels in the eastern Mediterranean.
G4529.emploi: Salamis appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 13:5, during the first missionary journey of Paul and Barnabas. The account indicates that this was the first place they preached after leaving Antioch of Syria, highlighting its strategic importance as a main stop for accessing the island of Cyprus.

sens: Place where John baptized, near Aenon
G4530.detail: Salim is a small village or region in Palestine mentioned only once in the New Testament. John chose this place to baptize because there was much water nearby — a necessary condition for administering baptism by immersion. The text specifies that John "was baptizing at Aenon, near Salim" (John 3:23), indicating that Salim served as a geographical landmark to locate Aenon, a baptism site likely situated in Judea.
G4530.origine: The name Salim comes from Hebrew and means "peace" or "tranquil." It is a Palestinian geographical name from the time, designating a peaceful place where water was abundantly available.
G4530.emploi: Salim appears only once in the entire Bible, in John 3:23. The evangelist John mentions this place to explain where John the Baptist was carrying out his baptismal ministry. The context shows that the presence of abundant water was an important criterion for choosing a baptism site, and Salim was located near Aenon, a region known for its springs.

sens: Physically shake, agitate with a violent movement
Make tremble, make unstable (a structure, a foundation)
Disturb someone's assurance and peace
Hinder, divert from truth or trust
Stir up, agitate (a crowd, doubts)
G4531.detail:
1. The primary meaning of the word is literal: to shake or agitate something by an external force. A reed "shaken" by the wind (Matthew 11:7) is the simplest image, just like a ship shaken by the waves or a measure of grain that is stirred to pack it down (Luke 6:38 speaks of pouring a measure that is "shaken").

2. The word applies to constructions or realities that lose their stability. A house cannot be "shaken" if its foundations are solid (Luke 6:48), while during an earthquake, buildings "tremble" (Acts 4:31) and even the earth itself can be shaken.

3. It describes the psychological and moral effect of a disturbance: losing one's peace, assurance in faith. The Thessalonians should not be "shaken" by false doctrines about the day of the Lord (2 Thessalonians 2:2) — that is, they should not lose their confidence and good judgment.

4. The word can mean "to make unstable" or "to cause to stagger": the powers of heaven will be "shaken" before the end of times (Luke 21:26, Mark 13:25), which expresses their loss of power and permanence.

5. Finally, it means "to stir up" a crowd or spirits to rise against someone: the Jews in Thessalonica "stirred up" the crowd in the city to oppose Paul (Acts 17:13).
G4531.origine: The word σαλεύω comes from the root σάλος (sálos), which evokes oscillation, swaying, hence the idea of unstable movement. In Hebrew, it often translates verbs like מוּט ("to stagger, tremble") or זוּעַ ("to be shaken"), which describe a physical or moral shaking. The family of σαλεύω includes terms for "salt" (σάλος as "salty agitation" of the waves) and expresses everywhere this notion of loss of balance, whether material or spiritual.
G4531.emploi: The verb appears 14 times in the New Testament, mostly in the Gospels and in Paul. It first describes violent natural phenomena: the wind shakes a reed (Matthew 11:7), a flood shakes a house (Luke 6:48), an earthquake shakes the building where the apostles pray (Acts 4:31). It is also used for signs of the end: the powers of heaven will be shaken (Mark 13:25, Luke 21:26). On a moral and spiritual level, Paul uses it to warn against any attempt to disturb the faith of believers (2 Thessalonians 2:2). Hebrews 12:26-27 plays on this double meaning: God shakes not only the earth but also "what can be shaken," that is, everything that lacks eternal solidity, while His kingdom remains unshakeable.
G4531.portee: This word reminds Christians that their faith must be founded on the unshakeable rock of Christ, not on wavering beliefs. It invites vigilance: to be spiritually shaken is to lose one's confidence and assurance in God. Finally, it proclaims a deep truth: earthly powers and even the visible heavens may stagger, but the kingdom of God is established for eternity.

sens: Ancient city ruled by Melchizedek
Symbolic place of peace and justice
G4532.detail: Salem is an ancient city in Canaan, famous in Scripture as the seat of the king-priest Melchizedek. According to Hebrews 7:1, Melchizedek was king of Salem and priest of the Most High God; he met Abraham returning victorious from the battle against the kings and blessed him. The name Salem means "peace" (Hebrews 7:2), which gives this city a symbolic dimension: it is presented not only as a historical city but as the kingdom of the king of peace, Melchizedek, who embodied justice and peace before the Law of Moses. This geographical site thus becomes a type or foreshadowing of the eternal peace brought by Christ, to whom Melchizedek is compared in the Epistle to the Hebrews.
G4532.origine: The word Salem comes from the Hebrew Shalom (שָׁלֵם), which means "peace." It is the same Hebrew term that is expressed in Greek as Σαλήμ in the Septuagint and in Hebrew by the root of shalom, peace. This city is most likely the ancient Jerusalem, as the two names — Salem (peace) and Jerusalem (foundation of peace) — denote the same concept of peace, and it is there that David and his successors established the seat of the kingdom of God.
G4532.emploi: Salem appears twice in the New Testament, only in the Epistle to the Hebrews (7:1-2), where Paul (or the author) develops the mysterious figure of Melchizedek. In 7:1, Salem is simply named as the political and religious seat of this king-priest. In 7:2, the author explicates the meaning of the city's name: Salem means peace, emphasizing that Melchizedek was king of peace. This restricted but intense usage shows that Salem is not mentioned for its ordinary geographical or historical characteristics, but for its connection with Melchizedek and for its symbolic charge: it represents the place where justice and peace reign.
G4532.portee: Salem reminds the believer that true peace emanates from a just royalty — that of Melchizedek and, by extension, that of Christ. By discovering this ancient city and its enigmatic king in Hebrews 7, the reader understands that God has always desired to establish a reign of peace and justice, long before the Law. This name of peace invites us to seek in Jesus the true king of peace, who accomplished what Melchizedek foreshadowed.

sens: Ancestor of Jesus from the people of Israel
Father of Boaz
G4533.detail: Salmon is a figure from the Old Testament who appears in the genealogy of Jesus reported by Matthew. He is the son of Nahshon (Matthew 1:4) and the father of Boaz, whom he had with Rahab, the woman who hid the Israelite spies before the conquest of Canaan (Matthew 1:5). His Hebrew name, Salmôn, also appears in Psalm 92 and the book of Ruth, where he is identified as an influential man from Bethlehem.
G4533.origine: The Hebrew name שַׂלְמוֹן (Salmôn) likely means "garment" or "clothing." This name appears in the Old Testament in relation to the family of Judah and the lineage of David, since Boaz, his son, is the direct ancestor of King David.
G4533.emploi: Salmon appears only in the genealogy of Jesus in Matthew 1:4-5, that is, in the list of ancestors leading from David to Jesus Christ. Matthew includes him precisely because he is the father of Boaz and the husband of Rahab: the latter, although non-Israelite (she was a resident of Jericho), is mentioned by name, highlighting how God has integrated outsiders into the lineage of the Messiah. Luke also mentions this figure in his own genealogy in Luke 3:32.
G4533.portee: The presence of Salmon in the genealogy of Jesus reminds us that the Messiah descends from ordinary and often imperfect ancestors: Salmon himself, son of an officer in the desert camp system, becomes a link in a chain that leads to the Savior. His marriage to Rahab shows that God welcomes into His plan the marginalized and outsiders who believe in Him: it is a promise for all who turn to Christ, regardless of their origin.

sens: Cape or promontory on the east of Crete
G4534.detail: Salmone is a rocky cape that juts into the sea at the eastern tip of the island of Crete. The ship carrying Paul and his companions to Rome sails past it: the text says they "reached the height of Salmone," meaning they passed near this land point and had to navigate around it to continue their journey in the Mediterranean.
G4534.origine: The name Salmone designates a real geographical location from antiquity. It is a well-known cape to Mediterranean navigators of biblical times, located at the eastern tip of Crete. The Greek text uses the same name as contemporary Greek geographers and sailors.
G4534.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 27:7, in the account of Paul's journey to Rome by ship. This episode describes the challenges of a difficult sea crossing, and Salmone is among the coastal landmarks that the ship must navigate. The precise mention of this cape shows the author's knowledge of actual maritime routes.

sens: Tumultuous movement of waves that rise and fall
Agitation, violent trouble
Signs of cosmic instability and fear among the peoples
G4535.detail:
1. The word refers to the violent and agitated movement of the sea waves, as they rise, roll, and crash against each other. It is the image of a raging sea, where the waters rise in powerful waves. In Luke 21:25, Jesus speaks of the roar of the sea and the waves as signs of the end times.
2. Figuratively, the word evokes agitation, trouble, and violent upheaval of a situation. The waves of the sea become an image of chaos and instability.
3. In the apocalyptic text of Luke 21, the waves symbolize the fear of the peoples in the face of great cosmic changes: when nations do not know what to do at the sound of the sea and the waves, it is a sign that the order of the world is shaken and that anxiety grips humanity.
G4535.origine: The Greek word σάλος comes from a root expressing the movement of swaying and tumult. In Hebrew, it often translates מוֹט (mot), which means to sway, to agitate. The family of the Greek word includes other terms related to agitation and shaking. The central image is that of violent and involuntary movement, like when a boat is tossed from side to side by the waves.
G4535.emploi: The word σάλος appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 21:25, in Jesus' eschatological discourse about the signs of the end times. Jesus describes the cosmic and earthly upheavals that will precede his return. The wave of the sea here is not just a natural agitation: it is an extraordinary phenomenon accompanied by the roar of the sea, which fills the nations with anxiety and leaves them in uncertainty. The context shows that the waves are among the major eschatological signs, along with signs in the sun, moon, and stars.
G4535.portee: This word reminds us that in biblical thought, the sea and its waves are symbols of destructive power and chaos. For the Christian reading this passage, the waves evoke both God's judgment on a rebellious world and, for those who hope in Christ, the certainty that these troubles precede his glorious coming. It is a call not to fear in the face of the upheavals of the world, but to recognize the signs of the Lord's proximity.

sens: brass wind instrument producing a bright sound
acoustic signal intended to alert or command
sound produced by this instrument
divine call announcing an eschatological event
G4536.detail:
1. The trumpet is a brass musical instrument used in the military to give orders and in religious ceremonies. Its bright and recognizable sound allowed soldiers to understand combat tactics or for the faithful to gather for worship.
2. The word also refers to the order or signal itself that the trumpet conveys: in 1 Corinthians 14:8, if the trumpet "gives an uncertain sound, who will prepare for battle?" — it is the precise sound that communicates an intention.
3. In eschatological passages, the trumpet becomes the symbol of a solemn divine call: in 1 Thessalonians 4:16, "with the trumpet of God," the Lord will descend from heaven and the dead will rise. In 1 Corinthians 15:52, "at the last trumpet," the dead will be raised incorruptible and the living will be transformed. It is no longer just an object, but a cosmic signal marking God's intervention at the end of times.
G4536.origine: The Greek word σάλπιγξ comes from a root expressing the idea of a loud noise. It primarily translates in biblical Greek the Hebrew שׁוֹפָר (shophar, "ram's horn") and חֲצֹצְרָה (hatsotsrah, "metal trumpet"). These two instruments played important roles in the religious and military life of Israel: the shophar sounded during great solemnities or to summon the people, while the hatsotsrah was more the instrument of the priests. Greek borrowed this term to designate any instrument producing this type of sound signal.
G4536.emploi: The word appears 11 times in the New Testament, particularly in Revelation (8 occurrences) and in the Pauline epistles. The concrete uses are few: in 1 Corinthians 14:8, Paul uses it as an image of clear communication. But from the Gospels and especially in the epistles and Revelation, the trumpet becomes eschatological — it announces the Parousia and the resurrection. In Matthew 24:31, the angels gather the elect "with a loud trumpet." In Revelation, the seven trumpets (4:1, 8:2 and following) announce God's judgments on the earth. This progression shows that the word moves from concrete military and religious use to a prophetic and apocalyptic sense.
