G4536.portee: For the Christian, the trumpet of God becomes a symbol of the irresistible divine call and the hope of resurrection. Hearing about the "trumpet of God" (1 Thessalonians 4:16) or the "last trumpet" (1 Corinthians 15:52) reminds us that the history of the world and that of each believer are not left to chance: they await a decisive event, joyful for the faithful, where God himself intervenes. It is an invitation to vigilance and trust in the promise of Christ.

sens: To produce a sound with a trumpet, a wind musical instrument.
To give a sound signal to gather, warn, or announce something.
To make something publicly known, to shout it from the rooftops.
Figuratively, to manifest or proclaim something in a striking manner.
G4537.detail:
1. To sound the trumpet means to make this instrument resonate by blowing into it. This is the simple and concrete action that the seven angels perform on the day of judgment in Revelation: "The seven angels who had the seven trumpets prepared to sound them" (Revelation 8:6). With each sounding, a catastrophic event occurs — a third of the sea turns to blood (Revelation 8:8), a third of the sun is darkened (Revelation 8:12). The sound of the trumpet marks a turning point in the course of history.
2. To sound the trumpet can mean to give a public signal intended to gather people or to warn them of imminent danger. This was a common practice in antiquity: the trumpet was sounded to summon the crowd, to announce a proclamation, or to signal a serious event.
3. By extension, the verb takes on a figurative meaning: "to sound the trumpet" means to make something public, to shout it openly. Jesus criticizes the hypocrites who perform their almsgiving by sounding the trumpet before them in the synagogues — that is, who do everything to ensure that everyone sees and knows what they are doing (Matthew 6:2). The image is that of a town crier announcing news in the public square.
4. More broadly, sounding the trumpet symbolizes the solemn and irresistible proclamation of a major event. When the seventh angel sounds the trumpet, "the mystery of God will be fulfilled" (Revelation 10:7): the sound of the eschatological trumpet marks the completion of the ages.
G4537.origine: The Greek verb σαλπίζω comes from the noun σάλπιγξ, "trumpet" — a long, straight brass instrument used by the Hebrews and neighboring peoples for military signals and ceremonies. In Hebrew, the verb תָּקַע (tāqa), "to strike" or "to sound (a trumpet)," was used to denote this action. The trumpet itself was called חֲצוֹצְרָה (ḥăṣôṣərāh) or שׁוֹפָר (shôfār). The Greek verb salpizō regularly translates the Hebrew verb תָּקַע in the ancient Greek version of the Bible.
G4537.emploi: The verb appears 12 times in the New Testament, almost exclusively in Revelation (9 occurrences: Revelation 8:6, 7, 8, 10, 12, 13; 9:1, 13; 10:7; 11:15). It is the decisive moment of divine judgment: each time an angel sounds the trumpet, terrible plagues fall upon the earth and the sea. In 1 Corinthians 15:52, the verb is used impersonally to signify the last trumpet that will sound at the final resurrection. In Matthew 6:2, Jesus uses it figuratively to criticize the ostentation of hypocrites who "sound the trumpet" before giving alms, that is, who seek to attract public attention to their good works. The context varies: eschatological in Revelation, moral in Matthew.
G4537.portee: This word reminds us that God acts in a striking and irresistible manner: the trumpet is not a discreet sound, but a call that resounds and compels listening. It also symbolizes the public and official nature of divine intervention. For the believer, sounding the trumpet in the Matthean sense (showing off) is a trap: seeking human glory instead of serving God in secret. The eschatological trumpet of Revelation reminds us that God controls history and that the final judgment will come with power and clarity.

sens: Musician who plays the trumpet
By extension, any musician or artist engaged in a profession related to music and the arts
G4538.detail:
1. A trumpeter is primarily a musician specialized in playing the trumpet, this wind musical instrument that produces bright and powerful sounds. He is a craftsman of sound and music, trained to master his instrument. In Revelation 18:22, he is at the heart of a prophetic vision: God lists all the musicians and artisans who will disappear when Babylon, the great city, is destroyed.
2. By extension, the word more broadly designates musicians in general and artisans of artistic trades: it represents the joy, beauty, and cultural life of a civilization. When John describes the fall of Babylon, the absence of trumpeters symbolizes not only the silence after the festive noise but also the end of all human activity, pleasure, and material prosperity.
G4538.origine: The Greek word σαλπιστής comes from σάλπιγξ (salpinx), which means "trumpet." It is an ancient instrument, widely used in military and religious contexts in Greece and the East, but also in festivals and celebrations. The suffix -ιστής (-istēs) indicates one who practices a trade or activity with this instrument — it is the mark of a specialist or artisan. The word shares the same root as other biblical terms like "to sound the trumpet" and connects to late Greek vocabulary and inscriptions.
G4538.emploi: This word appears only once in the entire New Testament: in Revelation 18:22. It is found in a prophetic description of the fall of Babylon, where John lists the audible witnesses of past prosperity and final silence: "the harpists, musicians, flute players, and trumpeters." These listed trades represent the entirety of the arts and entertainment, symbols of the luxurious and carefree life led by the inhabitants of that city. The apocalyptic context shows that divine judgment leaves no room for art or earthly joy.
G4538.portee: For the Christian reader, the trumpeter in Revelation 18 reminds us that all human glory, everything that seems beautiful and prosperous here on earth, is fragile and fleeting. The disappearance of music symbolizes much more than a musical loss: it speaks to the vanity of earthly accomplishments and the illusion represented by a civilization built without God. It is an invitation to seek joys and riches that do not pass away.

sens: Woman present at the crucifixion of Jesus, who stood among the most faithful disciples
G4539.detail: 1. Salome is one of the women mentioned in the Gospel of Mark as having followed Jesus to the cross. She stands at the foot of the cross with Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of James the Less, looking from a distance at the Lord's final moments (Mark 15:40). She later appears on the morning of the resurrection, with the same companions, to anoint Jesus' body with spices (Mark 16:1). Her name means "peace" in Hebrew, but the Bible does not tell us more about her life or her connection to Jesus' family.
G4539.origine: The name Salome comes from the Hebrew שָׁלוֹם (shalom), which means "peace." Some ancient critics believed she was the mother of the apostles James and John, the sons of Zebedee, but the text of Mark does not clearly affirm this. She symbolizes the quiet devotion of the women who supported Jesus until the end.
G4539.emploi: Salome appears only twice in the Gospel of Mark. She is first named among the women who observed the crucifixion from a distance (Mark 15:40), and then she participates with her companions in the plan to anoint Jesus' body on the morning after the Sabbath (Mark 16:1). Mark systematically places her alongside Mary Magdalene and the other Mary, highlighting the importance of these three women as witnesses to the decisive events of the Passion and the first announcements of the resurrection. She embodies the faithfulness of marginalized disciples at that time.

sens: Region in the center of the Promised Land, between Galilee and Judea
Main city of this region, capital of the northern kingdom of Israel
Territory inhabited by the Samaritans, a people distinct from the Jews
G4540.detail:
1. Samaria is a geographical region of the Promised Land, located in the center of the territory between Galilee to the north and Judea to the south. Jesus must pass through there to go from Galilee to Jerusalem (Luke 17:11; John 4:4).

2. Samaria is also the name of the capital city of this territory, where Jesus meets the woman at the well (John 4:5-7). It was once the capital of the northern kingdom of Israel.

3. After the crucifixion, the disciples are commanded to bear witness in Jerusalem, Judea, and Samaria before going to the ends of the earth (Acts 1:8). Following the persecution after Stephen's death, the Church is scattered in Judea and Samaria (Acts 8:1), and the Gospel is proclaimed there with power (Acts 8:5).
G4540.origine: The Hebrew word שׁמְרוֹן (Shomron) and the Aramaic שׁמְרַיִן refer to this region and its capital. The name likely means "the watch post" or "the lookout," reflecting its strategic importance on the heights of the center of the Promised Land. In both Hebrew and Greek, the term refers to both the region and its main city.
G4540.emploi: Samaria appears 11 times in the New Testament, primarily in the Gospels and Acts. It is mentioned as a region to be traversed (Luke 17:11; John 4:4), where the city of Sychar with Jacob's well is located (John 4:5). It becomes an important center for the expansion of the Church after Pentecost: it is where Philip preaches (Acts 8:5-9, 14) and where the Gospel is established (Acts 9:31). It is also part of the itinerary of Paul's missionary journey (Acts 15:3).
G4540.portee: Samaria symbolizes the opening of the Gospel beyond religious and ethnic boundaries. Jesus meets a Samaritan woman and offers her living water, thus breaking down prejudices (John 4). The disciples, initially Jews, learn to bring the Good News to a people considered enemies or outsiders. This reminds us that Christ's love transcends human divisions and that the Gospel is intended for all people without exception.

sens: Inhabitant of the region of Samaria, north of Israel
Ethno-religious group despised by the Jews
One who practices charity and compassion towards others
G4541.detail:
1. A Samaritan is an inhabitant of Samaria, a region in northern Israel. Jesus forbids his apostles from preaching in "the cities of the Samaritans" (Matthew 10:5), indicating that it was a distinct people with its own cities.
2. In the New Testament, Samaritans are portrayed as a group that Jews rejected and despised. John explicitly notes: "Jews do not associate with Samaritans" (John 4:9). The term even becomes an insult: Jesus is called a "Samaritan" to mock him (John 8:48).
3. Through the parable of the Good Samaritan (Luke 10:33), the term symbolically refers to one who has compassion and practices love for others selflessly, in contrast to the religious figures who pass by. A leprous Samaritan alone gives thanks to Jesus (Luke 17:16), showing a faith that the other nine—likely Jews—do not have.
G4541.origine: The Greek word Samareitēs comes from the name of the region Samaria (Samarie in French), whose capital was the city of Samaria. Historically, Samaritans descended from the inhabitants of the northern kingdom (Israel) and from peoples that Assyria settled there after the conquest of 722 B.C. They were therefore not considered true Israelites by the Judeans, which explains the mutual disdain.
G4541.emploi: The term appears 9 times in the New Testament, always to refer to the inhabitants of Samaria or Samaritan individuals. Jesus initially excludes them from the apostolic mission (Matthew 10:5), but this prohibition is lifted after the resurrection (Acts 8:25). The woman at the well in Sychar, a city in Samaria, is one example (John 4:9, 39-40). The parable of the Good Samaritan in Luke 10 transforms the term into a symbol of kindness towards a stranger. The context varies: sometimes geographical and neutral (a town of the Samaritans), sometimes marked by prejudice (calling someone a Samaritan as an insult in John 8:48), and sometimes spiritual and positive (the leprous Samaritan thanking Jesus).
G4541.portee: The term Samaritan teaches the reader that religious and ethnic barriers do not prevent salvation and that true faith does not depend on belonging to a recognized group. Jesus uses a Samaritan as a model of charity and a Samaritan as an example of gratitude towards God, transcending the prejudices of the time. It is a call to see in every person, even those rejected or despised, a potential heir of the Kingdom.

sens: A woman from Samaria, a mountainous region between Judea and Galilee
G4542.detail: The Samaritan woman is a woman from Samaria, this region in the center of the Holy Land populated by Samaritans. John 4:9 presents her at the encounter at Jacob's well: she is a woman from this region, a descendant of the mixed population that lived there after the Assyrian deportations of the 8th century B.C. The term refers to both her geographical origin and her religious and cultural identity, as the Samaritans formed a community distinct from the Jews.
G4542.origine: The Greek word "Samareitis" derives from the name of the region of Samaria (Σαμάρεια in Greek, Shomron in Hebrew). This name originally designated the capital built by King Omri of Israel in the 9th century. The suffix -ῖτις indicates belonging to a place, as one would say "Judean" for a woman from Judea.
G4542.emploi: The term appears only once in the New Testament, in John 4:9, in the famous scene of Jesus' encounter with the woman at the well. This unique occurrence shows how John identifies this woman by her Samaritan origin, which was socially significant: the relationships between Jews and Samaritans were marked by ancient hostility and religious separation. The Gospel thus emphasizes that Jesus crossed the social and religious barriers of his time.
G4542.portee: This encounter transforms the understanding of Jesus' ministry: he did not limit his message to Israel or Judea, but approached those whom the Jews despised or rejected. The Samaritan woman thus becomes a symbol of the universality of the Gospel and of God's grace that reaches all peoples, regardless of race or origin. It is an invitation to the Christian reader to overcome prejudices and to receive the Good News for all.

sens: island in the Aegean Sea
G4543.detail: Samothrace is an island in the Aegean Sea, located between Thrace (the northern coast of present-day Greece) and Turkey. It is famous in antiquity for the mystery cults practiced there. It appears in Acts 16:11 as a stop on the apostle Paul's journey: on his way from Troas to Macedonia, Paul and his companions stop there for the night before landing the next day at Neapolis.
G4543.origine: The Greek name Samothrakē (Σαμοθρᾴκη) literally means "Samos in Thrace" — a combination of the name of the island of Samos and the coastal region of Thrace. The name indicates the geographical position of this island between the Greek world and Thrace.
G4543.emploi: Samothrace appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 16:11. Paul and his companions, having received a vision in Troas calling them to Macedonia (Acts 16:9-10), embark to cross the Aegean Sea. Samothrace is simply mentioned as a stopover port where they spend a night before continuing to Neapolis, the main port of Philippi. This concrete mention of intermediate locations gives this travel narrative remarkable historical precision.

sens: island in the Aegean Sea
G4544.detail: Samos is a Greek island in the Aegean Sea, located near the coast of Asia Minor. During his third missionary journey, Paul briefly stops there while sailing to Jerusalem (Acts 20:15).
G4544.origine: This is the Greek name for this island, whose history dates back to antiquity. It was an important intellectual and religious center in the Greek world.
G4544.emploi: Samos appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 20:15. Paul and his companions sail past the island of Chios, then head towards Samos, before arriving at Miletus the following day. It is simply a waypoint in the account of Paul's journey back to Jerusalem after his ministry in Asia.

sens: Prophet and judge of Israel during the transition to monarchy
Major figure of the Old Testament, recognized for his intercession and faithfulness
Representative of the prophetic lineage that announced the Messiah
G4545.detail:
1. Samuel is the prophet and judge who governed Israel at a pivotal time in its history, between the period of the judges and the establishment of the monarchy: he anointed the kings Saul and David, marking the transition from one form of government to another (Acts 13:20 mentions him as the end of the period of the judges).

2. He is recognized by the New Testament as one of the great figures of faith and intercession, whose prayer accompanied all the people of Israel: Hebrews 11:32 lists him among the great men of faith, alongside Gideon, David, and the prophets.

3. Samuel holds a prominent place in the chain of prophets who prepared the way for the Messiah: Acts 3:24 cites him as the starting point of the prophetic succession "from Samuel," with all those who spoke after him also announcing the days of Christ.
G4545.origine: The Hebrew name Shemouèl literally means "God has heard" or "The one whom God has heard," referring to the prayer of his mother Hannah who asked the Lord for a child. Samuel is a central historical figure of the Old Testament, whose ministry is detailed in the first two books of Samuel.
G4545.emploi: Samuel appears three times in the New Testament, always to remind of his prominent place in the history of salvation. In Acts 3:24, Peter invokes him as the first link in a continuous prophetic chain extending to Christ. In Acts 13:20, Paul designates him as the one who marked the end of the period of the judges, inaugurating a new era. In Hebrews 11:32, in the famous passage about the "cloud of witnesses," Samuel is among the heroes of faith, alongside the greatest names of the Old Testament, underscoring the esteem in which the New Testament held him.
G4545.portee: Samuel reminds the believer of the decisive role of a life fully devoted to listening to God and intercession. His presence in the gallery of heroes of faith (Hebrews 11) invites every Christian to seek, like him, to know the voice of God and to faithfully convey it, even in times of transition or upheaval. He is also a model of spiritual leadership in service to the people of God.

sens: Warrior and judge of Israel during the time of the Philistines
G4546.detail: Samson is one of the great judges of Israel, known for his supernatural strength given by God. Born to a barren mother through a divine miracle, dedicated to God from before his birth by the vow of Nazirite (which forbade him from cutting his hair), he embodied the power of the Spirit of God at a time when Israel was oppressed by the Philistines. His story, told in detail in the book of Judges (chapters 13 to 16), shows a man of extraordinary strength but also serious human weaknesses, who ends up captive, blind, yet regains his strength at his death to avenge Israel. The epistle to the Hebrews cites him among the heroes of faith (Hebrews 11:32), acknowledging his role in the history of salvation despite his failings.
G4546.origine: The Hebrew name שִׁמְשׁוֹן (Shimshôn) literally means "little sun" or "burning sun," an image of strength and brilliance. This name reflects the very nature of the character: like the sun, he illuminates and consumes. The meaning of the name underscores the contrast between the power God granted him and the spiritual darkness he fell into at times.
G4546.emploi: Samson appears only once in the New Testament, in Hebrews 11:32, where the apostle Paul lists him among the heroes of faith of the Old Testament. This verse places him alongside Gideon, Barak, Jephthah, David, and Samuel, recognizing him as a man whose faith achieved victories. Although his life is marked by moral failures and a lack of self-awareness, Paul mentions him to highlight that God used him despite everything, and that his final faith, at the moment of his death, placed him among the witnesses of the old covenant.
G4546.portee: Samson teaches the reader that God can use imperfect and fragmented people, whose lives are not exemplary from beginning to end. His name appears in the "cloud of witnesses" of faith, reminding us that spiritual greatness does not depend on moral perfection, but on trust in God at the decisive moment. It is a call not to judge or abandon those whose trajectory is chaotic, for God can restore and use them for His glory.

sens: Light shoe covering the foot, secured by straps
Traveler's and walker's equipment in the ancient world
Sign of freedom and personal dignity
G4547.detail:
1. A sandal is a very simple and light shoe, consisting of a sole attached to the foot by straps or thongs. It is characteristic of the ancient East. In Mark 6:9, Jesus sends his apostles "shod with sandals" to proclaim the Gospel: it is basic, ordinary equipment, without luxury.
2. Sandals are the practical equipment of one who must walk and travel. In Acts 12:8, when the angel tells Peter "put on your belt and your sandals," he is preparing him to quickly flee his prison, to move freely. It is the accessory of movement.
3. Wearing or removing sandals meant something: removing sandals was a gesture of humility or respect (like taking off shoes on sacred ground). Having them on one's feet indicated freedom of movement and autonomy. The apostles thus receive the equipment of a servant who can go anywhere.
G4547.origine: The Greek word σανδάλιον is a diminutive of the word σάνδαλον, which probably comes from Persian. It is a small sandal, an ordinary sandal. This short and familiar form suggests simplicity and accessibility: it is the shoe of everyone, not a rare or noble object. In ancient Greek, when translating the Old Testament, this word renders the Hebrew נָעַל (na'al), which also refers to the light shoe of the Near East.
G4547.emploi: The word appears twice in the New Testament, both in contexts of mission and movement. In Mark 6:9, Jesus tells his twelve apostles to take sandals when he sends them on a mission to heal the sick and proclaim repentance: it is the equipment of God's messenger, simple yet necessary. In Acts 12:8, the angel orders imprisoned Peter to put on his sandals along with his belt to flee: here again, sandals signify the ability to move, to act, to be free. These two uses show that sandals are linked to action, mobility, and the fulfillment of a mission.
G4547.portee: For the reader, the sandals of the apostles remind us that the Christian life is not a life of comfort or prestige, but of service and movement. Jesus equips His disciples with the essentials — not luxury — to go and carry the Gospel. It is a lesson in simplicity and detachment: we set out light, with what is sufficient, trusting that God provides. Sandals also speak of freedom: it is while shod that we can walk, act, and testify.

sens: A flat and elongated piece of wood
A part of a structure or a ship made from flat wood
A means of flotation or rescue
G4548.detail:
1. A plank is primarily a flat and long piece of wood, shaped from a sawn board. It is an everyday object found in construction or woodworking.
2. In a naval or architectural context, a plank refers to the structural elements that form the hull of a ship or the walls and structures of a building. It is worked wood that serves as building material.
3. When a ship wrecks, the planks of the ship become survival objects: the shipwrecked cling to them to stay afloat. In Acts 27:44, after the shipwreck of Paul's vessel, the sailors and prisoners "got on boards or on pieces of the ship" to reach the shore. Each plank then becomes a makeshift raft for survival.
G4548.origine: The Greek word σανίς comes from a root that designates worked and shaped wood. In Hebrew, the word לוּחַ (loûakh) also means "plank" or "tablet" and covers both construction wood and the tablets on which one writes. The Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament) uses σανίς to translate לוּחַ in passages that speak of the construction of the Tabernacle or ships, showing that this word designates worked flat wood in all these contexts.
G4548.emploi: The word σανίς appears only once in the New Testament: in Acts 27:44, in the account of Paul's shipwreck on the way to Rome. Luke reports that Paul and his traveling companions, totaling 276 people, found themselves in danger when the storm wrecked the ship on the coast of Malta. Faced with the imminent disaster, the only means of survival was to cling to the planks of the sinking ship or to floating debris. This context of extreme urgency and rescue shows how a simple plank becomes an instrument of temporary salvation. It is God who ensured that all would reach safety, as He had promised Paul.
G4548.portee: This word reminds us that in moments of extreme crisis, even the most fragile and improvised means — a simple plank — can become instruments of God's protection. For Paul and his companions, what could have been certain death turned into total deliverance. This encourages us to trust God even when everything seems lost, for His promise and faithfulness are stronger than any material refuge.

sens: The Apostle Paul in the New Testament, before his conversion and under his original Jewish name
G4549G.detail: 1. Saul is the original Jewish name of the Apostle Paul. In Acts, this name is used only at the time of his conversion, when the Lord Jesus calls him directly in Hebrew. In Acts 9:4, during his vision on the road to Damascus, Jesus cries out to him: "Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?" — this repetition of the name emphasizes the urgency and importance of the divine call. After this transformative event, Saul will bear the Greek name Saulos and be known by his Roman name Paul, but it is under the name Saul that Jesus first addresses him, recalling his Jewish identity and marking the turning point of his existence.
G4549G.origine: Saul comes from the Hebrew Shaoul, a very common Jewish name meaning "asked of God." It is the same name as the first king of Israel (see 1 Samuel). The name appears in Acts in its indeclinable Greek form Σαούλ, used particularly in direct speeches, when the Lord or His disciples address him personally. This form of transliteration shows that the author of Acts deliberately preserves the authenticity of the Hebrew language, attesting that Jesus spoke to him "in the Hebrew language" (Acts 26:14).
G4549G.emploi: Saul appears five times in Acts, always in contexts of conversion and direct address. In Acts 9:4 and 22:7, the Lord calls him twice "Saul, Saul" during his miraculous vision. In Acts 9:17 and 22:13, Ananias calls him "Saul, my brother" to instruct him and heal him of his blindness. Finally, in Acts 26:14, Paul recounts how Jesus spoke to him in Hebrew on the way. All these passages relate the same foundational event of his conversion and apostleship, hence the constant use of the name Saul in these accounts.
G4549G.portee: The transition from Saul to Paul symbolizes the radical transformation of the persecutor into an apostle. For the reader, this name reminds us that even one who fought against the Church with all his might could be seized by the grace of Christ and become a powerful instrument of the Lord. It is an encouragement to believe that no conversion is impossible, and that God calls each one by name with a specific and salvific intention.

sens: King of Israel in the 11th century, first monarch of the chosen people
Hebrew name of the Apostle Paul before his conversion and mission to the Gentiles
G4549H.detail:
1. Saul is the first king that Israel asks of God. The Israelites, tired of living under the governance of judges, plead with the prophet Samuel to give them a king like the other nations. God agrees and chooses Saul, son of Kish, from the tribe of Benjamin, to reign for forty years (Acts 13:21). He is a warrior king, called to defend the people.
2. Saul is also the Hebrew name of the great apostle Paul at the time of his conversion. Before receiving the Greek name Paul, which marks his new identity as a missionary to the Gentiles, he is called Saul. This name roots his story in the Jewish people from which he comes and whom he initially served zealously.
G4549H.origine: The name Saul comes from the Hebrew שָׁאוּל (Shaoul), which means "asked for" or "prayed for." This name fits perfectly for the first king, as it is given in response to the urgent request of the people. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it is first borne by the king of Benjamin, and then in the New Testament, it is the birth name of the Apostle Paul, marking his Jewish roots.
G4549H.emploi: Saul appears mainly in Acts 13:21, where Peter reminds the Jews of Antioch of their first request for a king. It is a historical reference to the fundamental character of the Israeli monarchy. The same name is borne by Saul of Tarsus, the persecutor of Christians who becomes the Apostle Paul after his encounter with the risen Jesus. Acts uses the name Saul when recounting his early days as a believer, then gradually the Greek name Paul prevails, symbolizing his transformation and new universal mission.

sens: Rotten, spoiled (of a fruit or tree)
Unfit for use, worthless (of fish or merchandise)
Corrupted, tainted in its nature
Perilous, harmful by its effects
Dishonest, ignoble (in a moral sense)
Vain, barren (of words)
G4550.detail:
1. The word first paints the image of a fruit or tree rotting: it is the opposite of good and healthy fruit. Jesus says in Matthew 7:17 that "every good tree bears good fruit, but the bad tree bears bad fruit" — here, "bad" refers to the tree whose internal nature is corrupted.
2. It also applies to fish discarded after fishing: in Matthew 13:48, the fishermen set aside "what is good" and throw away "what is bad" — that is, the spoiled or unfit fish.
3. The word takes on a broader moral sense: something is "bad" because its deep nature is tainted, marked by corruption. It is the opposite of what is healthy and right.
4. It designates what is harmful by its results: in Luke 6:43, "a bad tree" can only produce bad fruit, because evil comes from its root.
5. In Ephesians 4:29, "a bad word" is an ignoble, dishonest word that hurts instead of building up — it bears the mark of sin or selfishness.
6. The word also suggests a certain uselessness or barrenness: a bad word serves no good purpose, it does not communicate "grace" but rather injury.
G4550.origine: The Greek σαπρός (sapros) comes from a root that evokes rotting, decomposition. The word had extended, especially in later Greek, to anything that is corrupted, vile, or contemptible — synonymous with the word αἰσχρός (shameful) or κακός (bad) in a broad sense. It is a very vivid Greek color: it was applied to what is literally rotten before being applied to moral evil.
G4550.emploi: The word appears 6 times in the New Testament, concentrated mainly in Jesus' teaching on the purity of the heart. In Matthew 7:17-18 and Luke 6:43, Jesus uses it to contrast the good tree and the bad tree — a theme of Ecclesiastes: what we are on the inside produces what we are on the outside. In Matthew 12:33, he returns to the same image to show that it is the treasure of the heart that comes out through the mouth. In Matthew 13:48, the context is more trivial: the parable of the fishing net, where the bad fish are simply discarded. In Ephesians 4:29, Paul transposes the image to the realm of speech: a "bad word" is one that does not serve to build up. The adjective remains linked to the idea of a vitiated nature, of an internal corruption that manifests outwardly.
G4550.portee: This word helps the Christian understand Jesus' teaching on the root of evil: one cannot expect good from a rotten heart, just as one cannot pick good fruit from a sick tree. It is a call to inner transformation, to the renewal of the heart. For speech, this means that every word we speak reveals what we truly are — hence the importance of keeping our heart and mouth pure.

sens: Believing woman from the apostolic age, wife of Ananias
G4551.detail: Saphira is the wife of Ananias, a couple from the early days of the Church in Jerusalem. Together with her husband, she sold a property, but both conspired to keep part of the proceeds secret while pretending to give the full price to the Church (Acts 5:1).
G4551.origine: The name Saphira comes from the Aramaic שַׁפִּירָא (shappîrâ), which means "beautiful" or "pleasant." It is a name that once expressed a commendable quality, but in the biblical narrative contrasts with the cunning and dishonesty of which Saphira became an accomplice.
G4551.emploi: Saphira appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 5:1. She is mentioned as the wife of Ananias during the sale of their property. Her story is set in the context of the early days of the Church in Jerusalem, where believers sold their possessions to help the less fortunate. The account shows how she shared in her husband's guilt in this lie against the Holy Spirit, leading to their divine condemnation.
G4551.portee: The story of Saphira reminds the reader that God sees the heart and knows hidden intentions, even within the community of believers. It is a warning against hypocrisy and deceit, especially when one pretends to serve generously. It invites sincerity and integrity in our commitment to God and the Church.

sens: Precious stone of blue color
Material used to adorn the heavenly foundations
G4552.detail:
1. The sapphire is a precious stone of a beautiful blue color, highly valued in antiquity as a luxury and adornment element. It is a rare and costly gem that symbolized wealth and splendor.

2. In John's vision, the sapphire is among the twelve stones that adorn the foundations of the wall of the heavenly Jerusalem (Revelation 21:19): it is the second foundation. This precious stone, along with others like jasper and emerald, helps to represent the incomparable beauty and perfection of the kingdom of God.
G4552.origine: The Greek word σάπφειρος (sappheiros) takes from the Hebrew סַפִּיר (sappir) which designated a blue precious stone. This Hebrew term is itself borrowed from ancient Eastern languages. The sapphire was known and appreciated by ancient civilizations of the Middle East: it is mentioned in descriptions of the temple furnishings and the priestly garments of the Old Testament.
G4552.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Revelation 21:19. John mentions it while describing the heavenly Jerusalem in his prophetic vision: the sapphire is presented as the second of the twelve foundations of the wall, symbolizing the splendor and purity of God's city. This description takes up and enriches the images of beauty and wealth already present in the Old Testament, where the precious stone was associated with divine majesty and objects of worship.
G4552.portee: The sapphire, in John's vision, reminds the reader that heaven is not an abstract place but a reality endowed with concrete and indescribable beauty. This gem, one of the most beautiful and precious known to man, is but a shadow of the splendor that awaits the redeemed. It invites contemplation of God's glory and a sincere desire for this eternal communion with Him.

sens: basket or woven container
means of transport or escape
G4553.detail: 1. A basket is a container made by weaving cords together. It is a utilitarian object, sturdy enough to hold and transport things. 2. In 2 Corinthians 11:33, Paul recounts how he had to escape from Damascus by being let down from the top of the city wall in a basket: this usage shows that the container was large and robust enough to serve as an improvised means of escape, suspended by a rope.
G4553.origine: The Greek word σαργάνη comes from a root related to weaving and braiding. Its primary image is that of intertwined cords, from which it evolved into a basket or container made of these woven cords. It is a practical term, common in Greek daily life.
G4553.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Corinthians 11:33. Paul uses it to describe a key moment in his life: his spectacular escape from Damascus after his conversion. He was in danger and was let down from the city wall in this basket. This episode shows how Paul had to face dangers from the very beginning of his Christian service, and highlights the humility and fragility of his condition, he who was once a persecutor of Christians.
G4553.portee: This simple yet vivid detail of Paul's escape in a basket reminds us that the apostles experienced a life filled with dangers and challenges for Christ. It humanizes Paul and helps us understand the price he paid for his commitment. It is a poignant image of dependence on God and humble courage.

sens: Ancient city of Asia Minor, historical capital of Lydia
One of the seven churches of the Near East to which John addresses messages in Revelation
G4554.detail:
1. Sardis was a major city in Asia Minor (modern-day Turkey), famous as the ancient capital of the kingdom of Lydia. John mentions it in Revelation 1:11 as one of the seven cities where Christian communities exist.
2. In Revelation, the Church of Sardis receives a message of rebuke: although it enjoys a good reputation ("you have a reputation of being alive"), it is spiritually dead (Revelation 3:1). Only a few believers in the city "have not soiled their garments" and will walk with Christ in white, a symbol of purity and victory (Revelation 3:4).
G4554.origine: The Greek name Σάρδεις (Sardeis) refers to the historical city known to the Greeks and Romans. Sardis was famous in antiquity for its wealth, purple textiles, and gold, before being destroyed by an earthquake and gradually abandoned.
G4554.emploi: John mentions Sardis three times, all in Revelation: first in the list of the seven churches (1:11), then in the message addressed to the local church (3:1-4). The context reveals that the church in Sardis suffered from a contradiction between its outward appearance (reputedly alive) and its spiritual reality (dead). This critique suggests a stagnant community, lacking dynamism or true commitment to Christ, despite a semblance of respectability.
G4554.portee: The message to Sardis invites the believer to examine their own spiritual life: are we not at risk of resembling a church that has fallen asleep, satisfied with its past or reputation, forgetful of the vibrancy of the connection with Christ? It is a call not to confuse appearance with reality, and to seek an authentic faith marked by concrete works of faithfulness.

sens: Fine stone of red-brown or orange color, variety of chalcedony
Symbol of beauty and glory in the heavenly vision
G4556.detail: 1. The sardius is a precious stone of reddish or orange-brown color, hard and translucent, belonging to the family of fine stones. It is mentioned in Revelation 4:3 as one of the stones that characterize the appearance of the one who sits on the heavenly throne, alongside jasper and reflecting divine clarity. 2. In the vision of the heavenly Jerusalem (Revelation 21:20), the sardius is the sixth stone of the foundations of the wall, listed among twelve precious stones that adorn the city of God. It thus stands as one of the symbols of beauty, purity, and glory of the eternal dwelling of the redeemed.
G4556.origine: The Greek word σάρδιον (sardion) refers to the stone from Sardis, the ancient city of Lydia in Asia Minor, known for its deposits of this stone. It is close to the word σάρδης (sardēs), the name of the city itself. In the Greek Old Testament, the same word translates the Hebrew אֹדֶם (odem), a red stone used in Exodus 28:17 for the high priest's adornment, highlighting the ancient use of this stone in worship and dignity.
G4556.emploi: The word σάρδιον appears twice in the New Testament, both in Revelation. In the first verse (4:3), John describes the vision of the divine throne: the one who sits there has an appearance reminiscent of precious stones, including the sardius, which conveys the transcendence and majesty of God. In the second verse (21:20), the sardius is included in the enumeration of the twelve stones that form the foundations of the wall of the new Jerusalem, each bearing the name of one of the twelve apostles. These two occurrences belong to the apocalyptic and symbolic register, expressing heavenly glory.
G4556.portee: The sardius, like the other precious stones in the apocalyptic vision, invites the believer to contemplate the beauty and magnificence of the eternal dwelling that God prepares for His own. It reminds us that divine glory is both transcendent, inaccessible, and sumptuous beyond imagination. For the distressed disciple, these images of precious stones strengthen hope in the reality and splendor of the heaven that awaits them.

sens: precious stone combining red and white colors
G4557.detail: 1. The sardonyx is a precious stone characterized by the alternation of red bands (from the sardius) and white bands (from the onyx). It is a variety of agate, composed of distinct mineral layers that create a particularly appreciated colorful contrast. John mentions it in his Revelation as one of the twelve stones that adorn the foundations of the heavenly Jerusalem, which testifies to its value and symbolic importance in the ancient biblical imagination.
G4557.origine: The Greek word σαρδόνυξ (sardonyx) is composed of two names: σάρδιον (sardion, sardius, the red stone) and ὄνυξ (onyx, the white stone). These two elements refer to the two visible components of the stone, whose appearance combines the characteristics of both rocks. The Ancients observed this natural combination and created a name that exactly describes what is seen: the sardius united with the onyx.
G4557.emploi: The sardonyx appears only once in the Bible, in Revelation 21:20, where it is listed as the fifth stone of the twelve foundations of the new Jerusalem. John precisely enumerates twelve precious stones that symbolize the beauty, solidity, and holiness of the heavenly city. This context shows that precious stones hold eschatological significance, meaning they belong to the vision of the world to come and the final fulfillment of God's plan.
G4557.portee: The mention of the sardonyx in the description of the heavenly Jerusalem reminds us that the biblical vision of the restored world includes material and sensory beauty. This stone, with its two distinct colors, can inspire the reader with the idea of harmony composed of contrasts, or the thought that God loves to associate different elements into a beautiful and coherent creation. For the Christian, it is an invitation to contemplate the promised future splendor and to consider that God cares about beauty in all its forms.

sens: Phoenician city on the Mediterranean coast, in the land of Sidon
G4558.detail: Zarephath is a port city of Phoenicia, located in the territory of Sidon (modern Sarafand in Lebanon). Jesus mentions it in Luke 4:26 to remind that the prophet Elijah, sent by God during a great famine, was not sent to help the widows of Israel, but a foreign widow in Zarephath — an act of divine grace toward non-Israelites that shows that God transcends religious and national boundaries.
G4558.origine: The Greek name Zarephath transcribes the Hebrew צָרְפַת (Tsaraphath), whose root evokes the idea of melting or refining metal. It was an important commercial and manufacturing center on the Phoenician coast.
G4558.emploi: Zarephath appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 4:26. Jesus alludes to it to comfort His rejected compatriots: He reminds them that the God of Israel has always helped humble and faithful foreigners, like the widow of Zarephath who welcomed Elijah. This historical reminder reinforces the message of the Gospel: God's grace surpasses human expectations and prioritizes faith over lineage.

sens: Belonging to the body, to physical matter
Concerning material or temporal goods
Subject to the desires and passions of the body
Pertaining to human wisdom rather than God's
Opposed to what is spiritual or divine
G4559.detail:
1. The primary meaning is literal: carnal refers to what belongs to the flesh, that is, to the physical and material body. In Romans 15:27 and 1 Corinthians 9:11, Paul speaks of "carnal" or "temporal" goods (material resources, money, food) in contrast to the spiritual goods he has brought.

2. However, the word quickly takes on a very important moral and spiritual meaning: carnal describes an attitude, a way of living directed by the appetites and passions of the body, without respect for God. In 1 Corinthians 3:3, Paul reproaches the Corinthians for being "carnal" because they have jealousy and disputes — they allow themselves to be dominated by their human desires rather than by the Spirit of God.

3. It also designates everything that proceeds from human wisdom and strength without God's help. In 2 Corinthians 1:12, Paul says he did not use "carnal wisdom" to conduct himself; in 2 Corinthians 10:4, "carnal weapons" oppose the power of God. What is carnal is weak and insufficient compared to what is divine.

4. In 1 Peter 2:11, "carnal desires" are the desires of the body that wage war against the soul — the image emphasizes that the flesh leads us toward evil and away from our true good.
G4559.origine: The word comes from the Greek σάρξ (sarx), which literally means "flesh, body." It is a classical derivative in ancient Greek. The Hebrew word it often translates is בָּשָׂר (basar), "flesh," which in the Greek Old Testament also refers to the body, human weakness, and sometimes sinful humanity. In New Testament Greek, there are two related words: σάρκινος (sarkinos), "made of flesh," which is more physical, and σαρκικός (sarkikos), "pertaining to the flesh," which is more moral and spiritual — it is the latter that is used to criticize a way of life.
G4559.emploi: The word appears 6 times in the New Testament, exclusively in Paul and Peter's writings. Paul uses it particularly to describe two things: first, material and temporal realities (resources, goods) in contrast to spiritual goods (Romans 15:27; 1 Corinthians 9:11); secondly, and much more often, a guilty spiritual attitude — one that consists of being guided by carnal desires rather than by the Spirit (1 Corinthians 3:3; 2 Corinthians 1:12; 2 Corinthians 10:4). In 1 Peter 2:11, it specifically refers to the desires of the body that fight against the soul. The word is never neutral: it always carries an implicit or explicit criticism.
G4559.portee: This word challenges the believer about the true source of their life: it does not reside in earthly strengths, wisdom, or resources, but in the power of God and obedience to His Spirit. Recognizing that a thought, desire, or strategy is "carnal" (that is, human, fleshly, without God) is the first step toward change: it leads us to seek wisdom and strength in God alone, and to master our desires rather than being enslaved by them.

sens: Made of flesh, belonging to the body
Pertaining to the weak human nature, opposed to the Spirit
Dominated by carnal desires and passions
Dependent on natural forces rather than divine power
G4560.detail:
1. The literal meaning: that which is composed of flesh, of corporeal matter. In 2 Corinthians 3:3, Paul refers to "tables of flesh" — the human heart, made of flesh, becomes the place where God writes His law by His Spirit, in place of the stone tablets of the Old Covenant.

2. The limited human nature: "carnal" designates man in his natural condition, without the strength of the Spirit. In Romans 7:14, Paul says "I am carnal" to express his inability to fulfill the law by his own strength, his subjugation to sin.

3. Spiritual immaturity: in 1 Corinthians 3:1, Paul calls the Corinthians "carnal" because they behave like "children in Christ," jealous and divided — their faith exists, but it has not matured.

4. The weak ordinance: in Hebrews 7:16, the law of Moses is said to be "carnal" because it relies on external commandments and material sacrifices, while Christ's priesthood rests on "the power of an indestructible life."
G4560.origine: The Greek word σάρκινος comes from σάρξ (sarx), "flesh." The suffix -ινος indicates the material or substance of which something is made: just as "a clay pot" is "clay-like," what is "carnal" is made of flesh or pertains to the flesh. In Hebrew, it is בָּשָׂר (basar), also translated as "flesh," which refers to both the physical body and, by extension, human weakness and mortality before God.
G4560.emploi: This word appears four times in the New Testament, always in Paul or in Hebrews, to qualify what belongs to the natural human order. In Romans 7:14 and 1 Corinthians 3:1, it describes the state of the believer still dominated by carnal tendencies — not the absence of faith, but spiritual immaturity or weakness. In 2 Corinthians 3:3, it relates to the human heart as the seat of life. In Hebrews 7:16, it qualifies the law itself as weak and temporal. The word always emphasizes a contrast: between flesh and Spirit, between natural forces and divine power, between the outside and the inside.
G4560.portee: For the believer, "carnal" becomes a call to recognize their natural weakness and dependence on the Spirit of God. It is not a definitive moral condemnation, but an invitation to grow: Paul reminds the Corinthians that they are "carnal," not to reject them, but to urge them to mature. Recognizing that one is carnal means accepting that one cannot rely solely on oneself and must depend on the power of God.

sens: The soft substance of the animal or human body
The whole body of a living person
Biological kinship, family connection
Present life, material and mortal
Human nature in its weakness and limitations
The tendency to sin, carnal desires as opposition to God
G4561.detail:
1. Flesh is primarily the matter of the body: the muscles, the skin, all that composes the physical envelope of an animal or a man (1 Corinthians 15:39). It distinguishes the living body from bones and blood (Luke 24:39).
2. By extension, flesh refers to the entire body of a living person — not separated into parts, but taken as a whole (Ephesians 5:29: no one hates his own flesh, but nourishes and cares for it).
3. Flesh can also mean blood relation, kinship: "my brothers, my relatives according to the flesh" (Romans 9:3) means our close ones, our true families.
4. When one says to be "in the flesh," it refers to life as we live it now, on earth, limited and mortal, opposed to eternity (Galatians 2:20: "the life I now live in the flesh").
5. Flesh is also our human nature in its weakness: it is incapable of fulfilling the law of God (Romans 8:3), it knows suffering and limitation (Hebrews 5:7).
6. Finally, especially in Paul's Epistles, flesh becomes the seat of desires that oppose God: lusts, pride, selfishness (Galatians 5:16-17: "the desires of the flesh are against the Spirit").
G4561.origine: The Greek word "sarx" comes from a root that designates soft and living matter, in contrast to bone. In Hebrew, it primarily translates "basar," which has the same concrete meaning: the flesh of the animal that one eats, or the human body. The Greek family of the word also includes "sarkikos" (fleshly), used to describe what belongs to the material flesh or what is dominated by carnal passions.
G4561.emploi: The word "flesh" appears 129 times in the New Testament, very frequently in Paul. It first appears in its natural and concrete sense: the living body of a person or an animal (John 1:14: "the Word became flesh"). It also refers to kinship and family by blood (Romans 9:3, 11:14). Gradually, especially in the Epistles, the word takes on a moral and spiritual meaning: flesh becomes weak human nature, subject to sin, incapable of pleasing God by its own strength (Romans 8:4-9). Paul repeatedly returns to it to show the conflict between flesh and Spirit (Galatians 5:16-17). It is one of the key words of his theology: to live according to the flesh is to live distant from God and dominated by passions; to live according to the Spirit is to obey divine will.
G4561.portee: This word reveals to every Christian the real weakness of our human nature without God. The Bible does not despise the body — it even celebrates its union with Christ (Ephesians 5:29) — but it warns us: our flesh, left to itself, carries within it the inclination to sin. This calls us not to live according to our own desires, but to surrender to the Spirit of God. It is a word that brings us back to humility and dependence on God.

sens: Ancestor of Jesus in the genealogy of the New Testament
G4562.detail: Seruch is a character mentioned only once in the Gospel of Luke (3:35), in the genealogy of Jesus. He appears in the lineage that traces back from Jesus to Noah, as the son of Ragau and father of Phalek. This genealogy connects Jesus to the patriarchs of the Old Testament, showing his roots in the promise made to Abraham. The name Seruch is the Greek form of the Hebrew name Serug, also attested in Genesis 11 as one of Noah's ancestors.
G4562.origine: The Hebrew name שְׂרוּג (Serug) likely means "intertwined" or "branch"; it designates a pre-flood ancestor according to Genesis 11:20-23. Luke 3's genealogy takes this long genealogical chain from the Old Testament and converts it into Greek (Seruch) for his Hellenistic readers. Seruch represents one of the ten generations between Noah and Abraham.
G4562.emploi: Seruch appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 3:35. It is Luke who, in writing the genealogy of Jesus, includes all the important ancestors of the Savior, tracing back to Adam. This list shows that Jesus, although he is the Son of God, is part of human history and the fulfillment of the promises made to the patriarchs of Israel.
G4562.portee: The presence of Seruch in the genealogy of Jesus affirms that Christ legally descends from the lineage that God has chosen and blessed since the origins of humanity. It reminds the reader that the Incarnation is not an isolated event, but the culmination of a divine plan that spans all ages.

sens: Clean the floor by pushing dirt with a broom
Make disappear what is impure or unpleasant
G4563.detail:
1. To sweep means to clean the floor of a house using a broom to gather and remove dust and dirt. It is a domestic, daily gesture. In the parable of the woman who lost a coin, she "sweeps" her house to search for her drachma (Luke 15:8), and after the demon departs, the house is found "swept" and adorned (Matthew 12:44, Luke 11:25). It is also an act of preparation and order.
2. Figuratively, to sweep means to clean or make pure. When the house from which the demon has gone out is found "swept," it emphasizes that it is empty and prepared, ready to receive seven other worse spirits. The image of the broom removes the visible, but it also shows that an absence of God leaves room for evil.
G4563.origine: The word σαρόω is a late form of σαίρω, which comes from the root "sweep" in English (Indo-European root for sweeping, cleaning). The family of this word in Greek includes terms related to cleaning and purity. In Hebrew, the context of purification and order was expressed by other words, but the concept of cleaning what is impure holds an important place in biblical thought and in the Law.
G4563.emploi: The verb "to sweep" appears only three times in the New Testament (Matthew 12:44, Luke 11:25, and Luke 15:8), all in the Gospel of Luke or Matthew. It always describes a concrete domestic action. In Luke 15:8, it is about actively sweeping to search for something lost, an energetic and meticulous action. In Matthew 12:44 and Luke 11:25, the "swept" house contrasts with the previous state and emphasizes a preparation — which will be unfortunate, as the absence of the Lord allows evil to settle in. The verb is simple and descriptive, rooted in daily life.
G4563.portee: This image of sweeping the house reminds us of the importance of purity and order in our spiritual lives. Cleaning is not enough: a house emptied of evil without being filled with the presence of God remains vulnerable. This invites us to actively seek what is lost (the sheep, the coin, the son) and to fill our hearts not only with what is good to remove but with the living presence of God.

sens: Wife of Abraham and mother of Isaac
A woman of faith who believed in God's promise despite her old age
A model of submission and obedience in marriage
G4564.detail:
1. Sarah is the wife of Abraham. She received this name from God in Genesis 17:15, which means "princess." She is the mother of Isaac, the son that God promised to Abraham.

2. Sarah embodies faith in God who accomplishes the impossible: although barren and over ninety years old, she trusted that God would keep His promise to give her a son (Hebrews 11:11, Romans 9:9). She is cited among the heroes of faith in the Old Testament.

3. In the New Testament, Sarah serves as a model for Christian women: she obeyed Abraham and called him her lord, and she did good without fear (1 Peter 3:6). Her example shows how to live faith and submission in the home.
G4564.origine: The Hebrew name Sarai (שָׂרַי) originally meant "my princess." God changed this name to Sarah (שָׂרָה), simply meaning "princess," because she would be the mother of nations and kings (Genesis 17:15-16). This name change, like that of Abram to Abraham, marked a new status and a new vocation in God's plan.
G4564.emploi: Sarah is mentioned four times in the New Testament, always in a context of faith and divine promise. In Romans 4:19 and 9:9, Paul refers to her to illustrate how Abraham and Sarah believed in a humanly impossible promise — having a child at a very old age. In Hebrews 11:11, the author counts her among those who received strength to become parents. In 1 Peter 3:6, she becomes a model of conduct for believing wives. These passages show that Sarah is not a distant figure, but a woman whose trust in God and obedience inspires Christians.
G4564.portee: Sarah teaches the reader that faith in God does not stop at youth or favorable circumstances, but perseveres even in the face of the impossible. Her example shows that God keeps His promises and that patience in faith bears fruit. For women, she illustrates how submission and virtue can coexist with a current trust in God, not as passivity, but as a quiet strength rooted in His faithfulness.

sens: Coastal region of Palestine, area of fertile plains located between the Mediterranean Sea and the inland hills
G4565.detail: Sharon refers to a geographical area of the Palestinian coast, characterized by its fertile and lush plains. This name appears in Acts when Peter heals a paralytic in Lydda: the inhabitants of Sharon, from this neighboring region, hear of the miraculous healing and many convert to the Lord (Acts 9:35). It is a region conducive to agriculture and pasturing, known in the Old Testament for its beauty.
G4565.origine: The Greek word Sharon transcribes the Hebrew Sharôn (שָׁרוֹן), whose etymology evokes a flat or level area. This name historically designates the coastal plain between Jaffa and Carmel. The word has been taken as is from the Palestinian geographical vocabulary into New Testament Greek.
G4565.emploi: Sharon appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 9:35. Peter has just healed Aeneas, a paralytic in Lydda, and this miraculous healing spreads to the neighboring region of Sharon. The name is mentioned as a region whose inhabitants, touched by this miracle, convert to the Lord. It is a context of evangelization and growth of the early Church in Judea.

sens: The adversary of God and men, leader of the powers of evil
The spirit that incites sin and rebellion against God
The accuser who divides and sows doubt
The one who holds men in spiritual bondage
The being who disguises to deceive
G4567.detail:
1. Satan is the name that designates the major enemy of God and His people. The word literally means "adversary": it is one who opposes God and seeks to turn men away from Him. Jesus commands him to depart by saying, "Get behind me, Satan!" (Matthew 4:10), recognizing his role as a tempter to be fought against.
2. Satan is presented as the instigator of evil and sin among men. He acts underground: he inspires Judas to betray Jesus (Luke 22:3, he entered Judas to betray Him), he whispers evil thoughts into hearts (Acts 5:3, where he inspires Ananias to lie). He also divides his own troops, seeking to destroy his own kingdom (Mark 3:26).
3. Satan seeks to create discord and doubt among believers. Revelation describes him as one who slanders the saints (Revelation 2:9-10). He also represents the hostile power that keeps men in darkness and spiritual bondage (Acts 26:18).
4. Satan keeps some men bound to the slavery of sin. A woman is described as being held captive by Satan for eighteen years (Luke 13:16), an image of one who deprives men of freedom and salvation.
5. Satan uses deception and disguise to seduce. He transforms himself into an angel of light to better deceive (2 Corinthians 11:14), showing his lying and cunning nature.
G4567.origine: The name Satan comes from the Hebrew שָׂטָן (satân), which literally means "one who opposes, who contradicts." This word originally designates a human adversary (like an enemy of a king), before becoming the title of the ultimate spiritual enemy. The Greek adopted the Hebrew word and integrated it into its declension. In the Greek Old Testament, this term translates the Hebrew satân to speak of one who resists God and His plan of salvation.
G4567.emploi: Satan appears 34 times in the New Testament, notably in the four Gospels and in Paul's epistles, but also in Revelation. The word always refers to the same character: the spiritual enemy in person. In the Gospels, Satan is the one who tempts Jesus in the wilderness (Mark 1:13) and his human adversaries (Matthew 16:23, where Jesus calls Satan the one who contradicts Him). Paul depicts Satan as a cunning being who deceives believers (2 Corinthians 11:14) and tests them (1 Thessalonians 2:18). In Revelation, Satan is presented eschatologically as the adversary who will ultimately be defeated and cast into hell (Revelation 12:9, 20:2, 20:7). The context always shows that Satan acts either by deceiving, accusing, or persecuting.
G4567.portee: Recognizing Satan in the Bible prompts the believer not to ignore the reality of the power of evil, which is neither a simple current of ideas nor an absence of good, but a personal hostile will. Understanding that Jesus stood up to Satan and defeated him (Matthew 4:10) encourages the Christian to resist without fear. Paul reminds that God can deliver Satan into the hands of believers (Romans 16:20): this is a call to vigilance and trust in the power of Christ over the adversary.

sens: Unit of volume measurement used in the ancient Near East for dry goods like flour
Quantity of about one and a half bushels
Image of a small action having great effects
G4568.detail:
1. The *saton* is a unit of volume measurement practiced in Judea and Babylon for measuring grains, flour, and other dry goods. It corresponds to about one and a half bushels, or roughly 13 liters — a significant quantity, enough to make bread for a household for several days. In Matthew 13:33 and Luke 13:21, Jesus speaks of a woman who takes three *saton* of flour: this is a large batch, not a small recipe.

2. In the two identical parables of the Kingdom, the word does not only refer to the technical measure but suggests abundance and the importance of the action: a little leaven, invisible and minute, silently transforms three *saton* of flour into a huge quantity of risen bread. The concrete measure becomes the image of a hidden power that works from within and ultimately transforms everything.
G4568.origine: The Greek word *saton* comes from the Aramaic *sata'*, which corresponds to the ancient Hebrew *se'ah* (*סְאָה*). This Hebrew word is rooted in a common Semitic root that designates measures and containers. The word refers to a vessel or a standardized measure, probably a jug or a basket whose volume was memorized. It is attested in the Greek Old Testament (Haggai 2:17), where it translates the same notion of measurement in the context of harvests and offerings.
G4568.emploi: The word *saton* appears only twice in the Greek New Testament, in the same parallel verses: Matthew 13:33 and Luke 13:21. Both evangelists report exactly the same parable of the leaven, mentioning the three *saton* of flour. This lexical choice reveals that Jesus was speaking to Jewish and Aramaic-speaking listeners familiar with this unit of measure: three *saton* was a tangible and known quantity, not an abstraction. The Bible uses it only on this specific occasion to teach about the Kingdom: no measure of taxes, tributes, or stocks, but of mysterious transformation.
G4568.portee: This parable of the leaven and the flour reminds Christians that the Kingdom of God never begins in a spectacular way: it establishes itself invisibly and progressively, just as leaven works in the dough. The precise mention of three *saton* — a concrete, domestic quantity — brings us back to reality: the Kingdom acts in ordinary gestures, families, and daily work. For those with eyes to see and ears to hear, even the measures of grain become messages from God.

sens: Person: the young man who kept the garments during the martyrdom of Stephen
Person: the Jewish persecutor who ravaged the Church before his conversion
Person: the convert who received the name Paul after a divine vision
G4569G.detail:
1. Saul is first presented as a young man from Jerusalem alongside the witnesses of Stephen's martyrdom, holding their garments while they stoned him (Acts 7:58). This discreet detail marks his entrance onto the scene.

2. He quickly becomes a fierce persecutor of the nascent Christian Church, entering homes, arresting men and women to throw them in prison (Acts 8:3). His religious zeal drives him to ravage the community of believers.

3. His life changes during a divine encounter on the road to Damascus: struck blind, he hears the voice of Jesus and repents (Acts 9:1-8). His eyes are opened spiritually and physically, and he begins to serve Christ.

4. After his transformation, he preaches with power, confounding the Jews by demonstrating that Jesus is the Messiah (Acts 9:22). His gift for argumentation makes him formidable to his former adversaries.

5. He becomes a leading apostle, sent on a mission by the Church in Antioch with Barnabas (Acts 12:25, 13:1-2). His ministry extends throughout the Mediterranean world.

6. In Paphos, during his first mission, he is called Paul, a new name that officially marks his turn towards the nations (Acts 13:9).
G4569G.origine: Saul is the Greek transliteration of the Hebrew name Shaul (שָׁאוּל), which means "asked for" or "prayed for." It is the same name as the first king of Israel. The Greek "Saulos" faithfully retains this designation, which the Acts exclusively use during the period of the persecutor and the beginnings of his conversion. The name change to "Paul" (Paulos) occurs later and reflects Saul's transition from his past life to his new identity in Christ.
G4569G.emploi: Saul appears 15 times in the Acts, with all occurrences concentrated in chapters 7 to 13. The name always designates the same person: the persecutor who becomes an apostle. The early accounts (Acts 7-8) show him in Jerusalem, involved in Stephen's death and then ravaging the Church. The turning point occurs with his vision on the road to Damascus (Acts 9:1-8): covered in blindness, he must be guided by hand to the city. His eyes are opened after Ananias visits him, and immediately he preaches Christ with power (Acts 9:22), confounding the Jews. He joins Barnabas in Tarsus (Acts 11:25) and begins his missionary journeys (Acts 12:25, 13:1-2). In Paphos, he receives the name Paul (Acts 13:9), marking his official entry into Gentile ministry. After this, the French Old Testament no longer calls him anything but Paul.
G4569G.portee: The figure of Saul embodies a radical conversion: the one who breathed threats against the disciples becomes the greatest apostle of the Church to the nations. His story teaches that no one is too far from the grace of God, and that even the fiercest persecutor can be transformed by an authentic encounter with Christ. It reminds us that religious zeal without true knowledge of Jesus leads to error, but sincere repentance opens up a completely new future. By seeing Saul become Paul, the reader understands that the power of the Gospel does not reside in human strength, but in the divine grace that transforms hearts.

sens: The apostle Paul in his early years, before his conversion and afterward
G4569H.detail: 1. Saul is the Jewish name of the apostle Paul. It is under this name that he appears in the account of his conversion in Damascus (Acts 9), when he was still persecuting the disciples before becoming a believer himself. After his conversion, he continues to be called Saul for several years, as seen when he joins the disciples in Jerusalem (Acts 9:26), and then during his early missions (Acts 13:9 marks the moment when he takes the Roman name Paul, which he will keep from then on).
G4569H.origine: Saul comes from the Hebrew name Shaoul (שאול), which means "asked for" or "prayed for." It is a Jewish name also borne by the first king of Israel. Luke uses the Greek form of the name when recounting Paul's life in Acts, before mentioning his name change to Paul, the Roman form adopted during his missions among the Gentiles.
G4569H.emploi: Saul appears in the Acts from the beginning of Paul's conversion to the start of his missionary journeys. The two provided occurrences show Saul a few days after his experience in Damascus, regaining strength and seeking to join the disciples in Jerusalem. This is the transitional moment: Saul the persecutor becomes Saul the believer, before becoming Paul. The name marks this pivotal period in the Apostle's life.
G4569H.portee: Saul reminds us that the name change in Paul reflects a profound transformation: from violent persecutor to dedicated servant of Christ. This transition from the Jewish name to the Roman name also symbolizes the evolution of his ministry: first apostle to the Jews, he gradually becomes apostle to the Gentiles. It is an encouragement for every believer: an encounter with Christ can radically transform a life.

sens: Stop the burning of a fire or flame
Cease a light
Eliminate, annihilate something active or living
Figuratively, stop the action of the Holy Spirit
G4570.detail:
1. The most direct meaning: stop the burning of a flame or fire. In Matthew 12:20, Jesus will not extinguish the smoking wick — that is, He will not eliminate a weak or fragile life. The word describes the physical action of depriving fire of what nourishes it.
2. A fire that is never extinguished (Mark 9:48, 9:44, 9:46): this is a fire that cannot be stopped, eternal, that continues to burn without interruption. The image evokes permanent and irreversible destruction.
3. Figuratively, extinguishing the fiery darts of the wicked (Ephesians 6:16): stopping, neutralizing the attacks of the devil as one would extinguish fiery projectiles with a shield of faith. The word moves from physical fire to spiritual reality.
4. Quenching the Spirit (1 Thessalonians 5:19): stopping or suppressing the action of the Holy Spirit within oneself, preventing Him from acting. The Spirit is experienced as an active power that can be refused or blocked, just as one would extinguish a lamp.
G4570.origine: The verb σβέννυμι comes from a root that expresses the idea of stopping a combustion. In Hebrew, the word כָּבָה (kabah) carries the same concrete meaning: extinguish the fire. This Greek term regularly translates this Hebrew verb in the Greek Old Testament. The basic image is that of fire deprived of oxygen or fuel, hence the figurative extension to anything that is stopped or eliminated.
G4570.emploi: The verb appears eight times in the New Testament, always with the same core idea: the notion of stopping something that burns or acts. In Matthew 12:20 and Ephesians 6:16, it is a conscious and active act (extinguishing a fire, neutralizing an attack). In Matthew 25:8, Mark 9:44-48, it is often in the passive form: the lamps go out, the fire is not extinguished. The context of Mark emphasizes the eternity of judgment, where the fire can never be stopped. In 1 Thessalonians 5:19, the verb becomes spiritual: one can quench the Spirit by refusing His direction. The Letter to the Hebrews (11:34) mentions faith that stopped the violence of fire — a physical power neutralized.
G4570.portee: This word invites the Christian to a double vigilance. First, to receive the power of the Spirit and not to quench it through unbelief or rebellion: it is a call to obedience. Secondly, to understand that divine judgment — symbolized by this unquenchable fire — is real and irreversible. It is also a reminder that our faith has power: it can extinguish the attacks of the wicked (Ephesians 6:16).

sens: Render religious worship to someone, recognize them as God
Fear with respect, revere
G4573.detail:
1. Worship means rendering worship to a deity, recognizing a place of honor and power in one's life. This is what idolaters do in Romans 1:25 when they worship "the creature instead of the Creator": they give a creature the status and honor that belong to God alone. It is not simply an opinion; it is an act: to worship is to bow down before, serve, obey.
2. The word also carries the broader meaning of fearing with respect or revering someone: one fears their power, recognizes their authority. This nuance appears in the ancient usage of the word (in Homer) and persists: to worship is also to fear in a pious manner.
G4573.origine: The word comes from the Greek σέβας (sebas), which means "reverential fear" or "solemn respect." It belongs to the family of the verb σέβομαι (sebomai), "to honor" or "to venerate." These two forms (σέβομαι and σεβάζομαι) are very close and eventually have the same meaning in late Greek. The starting image is that of fear mixed with respect: one stands at a distance, lowers their eyes, bows before what surpasses them.
G4573.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Romans 1:25. Paul uses it to describe the idolatry of those who exchanged the worship of the true God for that of creatures. This unique occurrence in an explicit context of idolatry shows that Paul emphasizes the false and perverted nature of this worship: it is not God that is worshiped, but a creature. The term highlights that it is a deliberate religious act, a form of organized service, a serious transgression of the first commandment.
G4573.portee: This word reminds the believer that worship is not a vague feeling or a personal opinion, but a precise act: to recognize someone as God and render to them the worship that is due. It highlights the danger of idolatry, which consists of giving to the creature what belongs to the Creator alone. For the Christian, this means examining where their heart, energy, and loyalty truly go: that is where their true God lies.

sens: that which is venerated or worshiped
that which receives the worship and respect of a community
G4574.detail: 1. The word concretely designates anything that a person or people venerates as sacred and worthy of worship. It is the material or spiritual object to which worship is rendered: statue, altar, deity. In Acts 17:23, Paul sees in Athens "objects" of devotion — the altars and idols that the Athenians worship — and he highlights their absurdity: they revere without even knowing what.
G4574.origine: The word comes from the verb σεβάζομαι (sebázomai), "to respect, venerate," which primarily expresses reverential fear, then worship. The root carries the idea of turning away (as one turns away from a person worthy of respect), and it gives rise to several words of the same family: "sebaste" (venerable, a title given to certain cities), "sebastoi" (imperial guards). It is a pure Greek word, common in the Greco-Roman world to speak of religious practices.
G4574.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament. In Acts 17:23, Paul addresses the learned Athenians who fill their city with objects of worship — altars, temples, statues of gods. His discourse reveals that these "objects of worship" are meaningless: the Athenians worship without knowing. In 2 Thessalonians 2:4, Paul describes the man of sin who demands for himself the worship and honor due to God alone: he places himself above all that is worshiped, claiming to be the supreme object of worship. In both cases, the term highlights the absurdity and peril of directing one's worship elsewhere than toward the true God.
G4574.portee: This word invites the reader to examine what they truly honor and worship. Anything that absorbs our respect, dedication, and trust — money, glory, personal image, power — becomes an "object of worship." The Bible reminds us that true worship belongs to God alone. Recognizing Jesus Christ as Lord means refusing to place our objects of worship between Him and us.

sens: Religious title designating one who is worthy of veneration and respect
The Roman Emperor, particularly Caesar Augustus and his successors
G4575.detail:
1. The word σεβαστός comes from a root meaning "to venerate" or "to respect": it originally designates something or someone worthy of reverence. It is a solemn title that expresses supreme honor and dignity.
2. In the late Roman context, this term became the official title of emperors: it is the Greek equivalent of the Latin "Augustus." In Luke, the word applies to the Roman Emperor before whom Paul appeals in Acts 25:21 and 25:25, and to the "cohort of the Emperor" in Acts 27:1 — that is, the official escort of the Emperor in Rome.
G4575.origine: The word derives from σεβάζομαι (sebazomé), which means "to revere," "to honor with respect." The adjective σεβαστός thus primarily designates what is worthy of veneration. In late Greek, particularly among the Jews of the diaspora, the term was adopted to translate the Latin title "Augustus," the sacred name of the Emperor and his imperial dignity.
G4575.emploi: The word appears three times in Acts, always related to the supreme Roman authority. In Acts 25:21 and 25:25, Festus explains to Agrippa that he has ordered Paul to be kept in waiting to be sent to "the Emperor" (literally "the Sebaste"), to whom Paul has the right to appeal as a Roman citizen. In Acts 27:1, Luke mentions the "cohort of the Emperor" (σπείρα σεβαστή), the imperial military unit responsible for escorting prisoners to Rome. In all cases, the term underscores the supreme political and religious power of the Roman regime.
G4575.portee: For an ancient reader, the word evokes the absolute earthly power of Rome; for the contemporary Christian, it implicitly contrasts with the assertion that Jesus alone is Lord. Paul stands before the highest human authority of the known world, but Luke reminds us that it is God who directs the course of events — Paul will arrive in Rome, not to be definitively judged by the Emperor, but to testify there to the Gospel.

sens: To render worship, to adore a deity
To show respect or veneration to someone
To fear God, in the sense of respecting and obeying Him
To be pious or devout, to live in piety
G4576.detail:
1. To honor means to render worship to a deity, to show the respect due to Him through acts or words of veneration.
