In Matthew 15:9 and Mark 7:7, Jesus rebukes the Pharisees for honoring (God) with their lips only through human commandments, showing that true honor requires the heart and obedience, not empty ritual.
2. It also means to show respect or reverence towards someone, recognizing their authority or importance. The word designates this attitude of respectful submission that one manifests before someone considered superior.
3. To fear God means here to deeply respect Him, and thus to obey Him and remain faithful to Him. Lydia (Acts 16:14) is described as a woman who fears God: she lives to please Him and to listen to His word, which explains why the Lord opened her heart.
4. To be pious or devout is to live in this attitude of respect towards God, which translates into faithful conduct. In Acts 13:43, the pious proselytes follow Paul and Barnabas: their piety drives them to seek the truth and to cling to the grace of God.
G4576.origine: The verb σέβομαι comes from the root σέβ-, which expresses the idea of turning away, retreating with respect before something superior or sacred. In Greek, it is an ancient root word that has always retained this religious sense of reverence towards the gods. In the Greek Old Testament, it generally translates the Hebrew word יָרֵא (to fear, to dread), particularly used to express reverential fear towards God. This root has also given rise to the name σέβας (respect, majesty) and σεβάσμιος (worthy of respect).
G4576.emploi: The verb σέβομαι appears 10 times in the New Testament, always in the middle-passive form (reflexive). It is particularly frequent in the Acts of the Apostles, where it designates the attitude of those who recognize God or the gods: the Pharisees who worship God in words (Matthew 15:9, Mark 7:7), the proselytes and the "God-fearers" (σεβόμενοι) who are Gentiles gathered around the synagogue (Acts 13:43, 50, 17:4, 17), Lydia who fears God and listens to Paul (16:14), and the worshippers of the cult of Artemis (19:27). The word always designates a religious attitude: respect, veneration, obedience towards what one honors. This can apply to God Himself or, among polytheists, to idols and gods.
G4576.portee: This word reminds us that true religion does not consist of empty words or external rituals, but in a deep respect for God that transforms life. Jesus in Matthew 15:9 and Mark 7:7 criticizes those who honor God with their lips: true honor requires the heart, obedience, and sincerity. The term "God-fearer" (one who fears God) also designates the pious Gentiles who seek the truth and turn to God: it is an invitation to see that true piety is not reserved for one people, but is addressed to all who wish to listen to God and obey Him.

sens: Link of diverse nature, rope or chain, used to restrain or bind
Chain made of iron or other material, instrument of captivity
Figurative image of slavery or spiritual captivity
G4577.detail:
1. The word σειρά primarily designates any link capable of restraining: a rope, a line, or a chain. It is a material object that one wraps or ties around something. In Greco-Roman antiquity, it was also used for hair braided or tied in curls (Judges 16:13-14 in the Septuagint).

2. In the literal sense, the chain is the instrument of imprisonment and servitude. It is what chains a prisoner, immobilizing them and depriving them of freedom. It evokes the violence of capture and the harshness of imposed captivity.

3. Figuratively, σειρά symbolizes everything that chains the soul: spiritual slavery, the domination of evil, or divine punishment. In 2 Peter 2:4, it designates the chains of darkness in which God has plunged the rebellious angels, an image of the captivity of evil forces awaiting judgment.
G4577.origine: The word comes from Greek and etymologically designates everything that binds, restrains, or wraps. The root evokes the image of a flexible or rigid link that encircles. The Septuagint uses it to translate the Hebrew מַחְלָפָה (makhlapha, that which braids or wraps) and חֶבֶל (hevel, rope or link). This link can be material and visible, or become an image of spiritual servitude.
G4577.emploi: σειρά appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Peter 2:4, in what seems to be an ancient textual variant (« σειραὶ ζόφου », chains of darkness). Peter uses it to describe the divine prison where God has cast the angels who sinned, awaiting eternal judgment. This image belongs to the theology of judgment: the chains are not human, but cosmic and definitive. The usage is clearly metaphorical and eschatological, speaking not of the present but of the retention of demonic powers in dark captivity until the final judgment.
G4577.portee: This word reminds Christians that evil, in all its forms — whether angelic or human — does not escape God. The powers hostile to His reign are not only fought against but ultimately imprisoned and judged. This offers believers assurance: God's victory is complete and definitive. No one escapes His justice.

sens: a violent agitation of the earth
a sudden shock that shakes the foundations
a catastrophic natural phenomenon signaling times of crisis
a sign of divine intervention
G4578.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes the violent and involuntary movement of the earth beneath our feet when it shakes and trembles. It refers to the physical phenomenon itself: in Acts 16:26, a great earthquake shakes the foundations of the prison in Philippi so strongly that all the doors open.

2. It is a shock capable of damaging structures — walls, buildings, chains — and creating terror among those who experience it. When Jesus died on the cross, according to Matthew 27:54, an earthquake occurs, and the centurion and his soldiers, who witness it, are seized with great fear.

3. In the prophecies of the New Testament, the earthquake appears as a sign of times of distress and crisis before the end of the world: Jesus announces that there will be earthquakes in various places (Mark 13:8), among famines and wars, as "the beginning of sorrows."

4. The word can also refer to a violent storm at sea (Matthew 8:24), where the shaking of the waves covers the boat. But above all, the earthquake is perceived as an act of God: it intervenes to deliver (Acts 16:26), to testify to the power of Jesus (Matthew 27:54), or to manifest God's work in the heavens (Revelation 8:5, 11:19).
G4578.origine: The Greek word σεισμός comes from the verb σείω ("to shake, to tremble"), which expresses a sudden and violent movement. In Hebrew, the Old Testament uses רַעַשׁ (raa'ash) for earthquakes, particularly in accounts where God manifests His power (earthquakes during God's coming, or in the context of judgment). The Greek word thus applies to both natural realities (earthquakes and storms) and divine interventions.
G4578.emploi: The word appears 12 times in the New Testament, mostly in Matthew and Revelation. Matthew uses the term in his Gospel for contemporary events (the storm in 8:24, the earthquake at the moment of Jesus' death in 27:54, the one accompanying the resurrection in 28:2), and in the eschatological discourse (24:7) where earthquakes signal the end times. Mark and Luke report the same prophetic discourse of Jesus. Acts describes an earthquake as a miraculous liberating event (16:26). Revelation abundantly uses the word to describe the wonders accompanying divine judgments and opening eyes to the heavenly reality (6:12, 8:5, 11:13-19, 16:18). From one usage to another, the word retains its meaning of physical shaking, but it becomes the privileged sign of God's power and presence.
G4578.portee: The earthquake in the Bible is not just a natural disaster: it is often the signal that God is acting. For the believer, this word reminds us that God controls the physical universe and uses it to manifest His power, deliver His children, or remind humanity of the reality of the coming judgment. The earthquakes announced by Jesus invite vigilance and trust in Him rather than fear.

sens: To make something physically tremble or move
To cause a shock or vibration
To agitate or violently stir
To deeply disturb someone, filling them with emotion or fear
G4579.detail:
1. To shake primarily means to make tremble or move: it is a clear physical movement. When Jesus entered Jerusalem, "the whole city was stirred" (Matthew 21:10) — not merely in a sentimental sense, but in a true disturbance, a collective agitation. Similarly, at the crucifixion, "the earth shook" (Matthew 27:51), a real and visible shock.

2. The word can describe a gesture of violent shaking: in Revelation 6:13, a fig tree "shaken by a violent wind drops its figs" — it is the same verb, depicting the physical action of making something fall.

3. On the emotional and heart level, to shake means to deeply disturb, to fill with fear or inner agitation. The guards at the tomb "trembled with fear" (Matthew 28:4) — their hearts were shaken by fear in the face of the miracle. It is a disruption that affects the whole person.

4. The word also carries a spiritual significance: God shakes, disturbs the very foundations of things. In Hebrews 12:26, the Lord declares that He "shakes not only the earth, but also heaven" — it is divine judgment that reaches everything that stands, everything that seems solid.
G4579.origine: The Greek word σείω comes from a root that evokes back-and-forth movement, shaking. The Hebrew it often translates in the Old Testament (רָעַשׁ, raa'ash) also denotes trembling, vibration — especially that caused by God during His terrible manifestations. It is a dynamic action verb, always describing a violent or intense movement, never a tranquil one.
G4579.emploi: The verb "to shake" appears 5 times in the provided passages, always for moments of spiritual or physical importance. It is used in the literal sense: the earth shaking at Jesus' death (Matthew 27:51), a fig tree being shaken (Revelation 6:13). But it is also used for emotions: the city stirred by Jesus' arrival (Matthew 21:10), the guards trembling with fear (Matthew 28:4). In Hebrews 12:26, it takes on a cosmic and theological dimension: it is God Himself who shakes the entire universe. The context changes, but the heart of the word remains: a disturbance, an agitation that affects something or someone.
G4579.portee: This word reminds the reader that Jesus did not go unnoticed: His arrival, His death, His resurrection disturbed the order of things, troubled hearts, and even shook creation. It is an invitation not to remain indifferent: before Christ, every true believer must be "shaken," that is, touched, transformed. The word also depicts God's sovereign action, who alone can truly shake the world and call men to stand firm in faith.

sens: Companion of Paul on his journey to Jerusalem
G4580.detail: 1. Secundus is a man from Thessalonica who accompanies the apostle Paul on his journey to Asia towards Jerusalem around 57 A.D. (Acts 20:4). His Latin name literally means "the second," but it is simply a common personal name in Roman times, with no connection to an order of succession.
G4580.origine: The name Secundus is a Latin form meaning "second" or "second one" (from the Latin sequi, to follow). It was commonly given as a first name in the Roman world, particularly for children born after the first. In the context of the New Testament, it is an ordinary personal name, without special connotation.
G4580.emploi: Secundus appears only once in the Bible, in Acts 20:4, where he is mentioned among a list of disciples and companions accompanying Paul. He is part of the representatives of the churches in Asia Minor who travel with the apostle to carry the offerings of the churches to Jerusalem. Although little information is given about him in Scripture, his presence shows how local churches were concretely engaged in the apostolic ministry by sending their own delegates.

sens: Major coastal city of Syria, principal maritime port of the Seleucid empire
G4581.detail: Seleucia was a large port city built on the Mediterranean coast of Syria, about 25 km north of Antioch. It served as the main port for the Seleucid empire, one of the dominant powers in the Middle East after the death of Alexander the Great. It was from there that ships departed for maritime journeys to other regions of the Mediterranean, notably to Cyprus (Acts 13:4).
G4581.origine: The name "Seleucia" honors Seleucus I Nicator, founder of the Seleucid dynasty (around 312 B.C.). Several cities bore this name in the empire, but this one was the most important on the Syrian coast. It represented the commercial and political power of this Hellenistic period in the Middle East.
G4581.emploi: Seleucia appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 13:4. It is mentioned as the starting point of Paul and Barnabas's first missionary journey, sent by the Holy Spirit from Antioch. This mention underscores the strategic importance of this port for apostolic travels to the Mediterranean islands like Cyprus.

sens: the celestial body that shines at night and orbits around the earth
the light or brightness that the moon provides
a point of comparison to express brilliance or glory
a sign of the last days and cosmic upheavals
G4582.detail: 1. The moon is primarily the visible celestial body at night: in Luke 21:25, it is mentioned alongside the sun and stars as an observable element of the sky. 2. It also refers to the light it produces — this can cease or be altered: in Matthew 24:29 and Mark 13:24, "the moon will not give its light" describes its darkening during the signs of the end. 3. The moon serves as a term of comparison to measure the brilliance of things: in 1 Corinthians 15:41, Paul writes that "the glory of the moon" is different from that of the sun or stars, to show that each creature has its own glory. 4. In Revelation, the moon becomes a symbol of eschatological cosmic upheavals — it "becomes like blood" (Revelation 6:12) or darkens (Revelation 8:12), expressing the terrifying signs that accompany divine intervention at the end of times.
G4582.origine: The Greek word σελήνη comes from an Indo-European root related to the idea of shining or glowing, hence its meaning of "moon." In Hebrew, it is יָרֵחַ (yareah), whose original meaning is also "the one who shines"; the Greek often translates this Hebrew term in the Old Testament. The moon, in ancient cultures, was the natural symbol of nighttime light, ruling over the night as the sun rules over the day.
G4582.emploi: The word appears 9 times in the New Testament, mainly in eschatological texts. The first three Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke) and Acts use it when describing the signs of the end of the world, particularly in Jesus' eschatological discourse on the Mount of Olives. Paul uses it once in 1 Corinthians 15 to establish an analogy: each celestial object has its own glory, so our resurrected bodies will also have their own brilliance. Revelation, rich in celestial symbolism, mentions the moon several times: darkened, turned blood-red, or absent from the heavenly Jerusalem where God replaces all created light. In every context, the moon is never worshiped or deified, but remains a created element of the cosmos.
G4582.portee: For the Christian, the moon reminds us that everything that shines in this world — even what seems eternal and unchanging — remains a creation subject to God. The eschatological passages teach that cosmic signs herald the return of Christ and judgment, inviting the believer to remain vigilant. The image of the moon darkening or turning to blood also emphasizes that the visible and stable things of this world will not last: only the presence of God will endure.

sens: a person afflicted with epilepsy or a mental illness
a person thought to be affected by the phases of the moon
G4583.detail: 1. The word designates someone suffering from a serious illness affecting the mind and body — particularly epilepsy, with its sudden seizures. In Matthew 4:24, Jesus heals "moonstruck" individuals among many other sick people, and in Matthew 17:15, a father says his son is "moonstruck and suffers severely," describing his falls into fire and water. 2. The etymology reveals what the ancients believed: the word comes from "selene" (the moon), and reflects the popular belief that the phases of the moon caused or worsened these seizures. Although this explanation is false, the Bible uses the term to describe the reality of suffering, without adopting the superstition.
G4583.origine: The Greek word comes from "selene" (moon), forged on the ancient idea that the moon influenced mental and neurological illnesses. This belief was widespread in the Greco-Roman world: it was thought that full moons triggered episodes of madness or epilepsy. The word appears in the historian Manetho, before being adopted in the New Testament. Although the etymology reveals a superstition, the Bible uses it simply to name an observable illness.
G4583.emploi: The verb appears only twice, in two healing accounts in Matthew. In Matthew 4:24, it lists categories of sick people that Jesus heals: demon-possessed, moonstruck, and paralytics — the context shows that the term describes a recognizable physical and mental state. In Matthew 17:15, a father asks Jesus to heal his "moonstruck" son, describing severe symptoms: repeated falls into fire and water. These two passages show that moonstruckness was a real and serious condition, worthy of mention alongside other illnesses.
G4583.portee: This term reminds us that Jesus addresses the entirety of human suffering — mental, physical, and spiritual — and heals it. He does not judge people's superstitions about the causes; He comes to liberate from the illness itself. For us, this means that all suffering, even if misunderstood, falls within the realm of Christ's compassion and power.

sens: ancestor of Jesus according to his genealogy
descendant of David and Nathan
G4584.detail: Shemiah is a character mentioned only once in the Bible, in the genealogy of Jesus reported by Luke. He is situated in the Davidic line, a descendant of David through the son Nathan (and not through Solomon). According to Luke 3:26, he is the father of Josech and the son of Maath, placing him several generations before Mary, the mother of Jesus.
G4584.origine: The name Shemiah (or Shemei in Hebrew) appears in the Old Testament, notably as an adversary of David. This name literally means "the one who has heard" (from the root shama, to hear). It was borne by several important figures in the history of Israel.
G4584.emploi: Shemiah is mentioned only in Luke 3:26, in the complete genealogy of Jesus established by Luke. This ancestor is situated about fifty generations before Jesus according to Luke's account. He is part of the royal Davidic line that leads to the birth of the Messiah. Luke thus establishes the historical and genealogical continuity of God's plan from David to Jesus.
G4584.portee: This mention reminds the reader that Jesus is part of a real and verifiable genealogy, rooted in the history of Israel and the promise made to David. It attests that Jesus is indeed the son of David in a genealogical and historical sense, and that God has guided history in a precise and trustworthy manner to fulfill His promises.

sens: refined and finely ground wheat flour
precious and luxury merchandise in trade
G4585.detail:
1. Fine flour is a wheat flour obtained through very fine milling, more refined than ordinary flour. It was valued in antiquity for the superior quality of the breads and pastries made from it. In Revelation 18:13, it appears in a long enumeration of luxury goods: "cinnamon, spices, perfumes, myrrh, incense, wine, oil, fine flour, wheat..." This list describes the riches that Babylon traded around the world.
2. The context shows that fine flour is not a simple everyday food, but an expensive commercial product, a symbol of prosperity and refinement. It represents the material goods upon which an apparently powerful society depends—goods that, in John's vision, will disappear overnight at God's judgment.
G4585.origine: The Greek word semidalis comes from the Latin semidalis, which itself is borrowed from a Semitic language: it translates the Hebrew selet (סֹלֶת), which refers to the fine flour obtained after sifting and finely grinding wheat. This word illustrates how biblical Greek has enriched its vocabulary from the Mediterranean trade by borrowing terms for precious products from neighboring languages.
G4585.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Revelation 18:13. It is part of the lament over the fall of Babylon, where merchants weep for the loss of their precious cargoes. John lists all the luxury items that constituted the wealth of trade: precious metals, rare fabrics, spices, incense, and also fine flour and wheat. This mention places fine flour alongside imported and costly products, not as ordinary bread but as a high-status and internationally traded good.
G4585.portee: For the Christian reader, this word invites reflection on the ephemeral nature of material wealth and luxury. Fine flour, a symbol of refinement and prosperity in a great trading city, is rendered worthless in an instant. It is a call not to seek security or identity in the accumulation of goods, even precious ones, but to place trust in God alone, whose word endures forever.

sens: Worthy of respect and esteem due to dignity and seriousness
Deserving of consideration, trustworthy, eminent
Serious, reserved in behavior and demeanor
Inspiring respect through moral nobility
G4586.detail:
1. The word primarily describes what commands respect through its natural dignity—what is "august," venerable. It is the impression made by a person who carries their responsibility seriously, without frivolity. In 1 Timothy 3:8, deacons are asked to be "honorable," meaning trustworthy, inspiring respect through their moral gravity.
2. The word also designates the quality of what is serious, grave, eminent—whether it be a person or a thought. In Titus 2:2, older men are to be "honorable": sober, measured, worthy of consideration.
3. The word can also qualify a thing, a word, or a thought that bears the mark of dignity. In Philippians 4:8, Paul invites believers to focus their thoughts on what is "honorable": not on what is trivial or base, but on what has value and moral grandeur.
G4586.origine: The word comes from the verb meaning "to revere, to honor" (σέβομαι). It thus carries the idea of respect, veneration. It is a quality that evokes a natural inclination in those who see it to honor the person who possesses it. The root evokes what imposes respect, what has weight and dignity.
G4586.emploi: The word appears only four times in the New Testament, always in connection with moral qualities expected of Christians in authority (deacons, elders, women) or in ordinary life. In 1 Timothy 3:8 and 3:11, it describes the behavior of deacons and the women who assist them—they must be honorable, meaning serious and trustworthy. In Titus 2:2, it is a quality expected of older men. In Philippians 4:8, Paul uses it more broadly to qualify thoughts themselves: fixing the mind on what is honorable means cultivating worthy, serious, morally valuable thoughts.
G4586.portee: This word reminds the Christian that a life of faith does not hide or shrink: it shines through its seriousness, stability, and moral dignity. For one who wishes to serve the Church or simply live as a disciple, honorability—understood as gravity worthy of respect—is not a minor virtue: it is what makes credible and legitimate all that one says and does. Cultivating honorability is cultivating a life that bears witness to Christ through its very solidity.

sens: serious and respectable behavior
grave and majestic character
dignity of one who inspires respect
irreproachable presentation in conduct
G4587.detail:
1. Honesty is primarily a serious and dignified demeanor: it is the behavior of someone who carries themselves well, inspiring trust through their appearance and manners. In 1 Timothy 3:4, it is required that one who leads the Church keeps their children "in perfect honesty"—that is, with calm and respectful authority, not loud or disorderly.
2. It is also the natural dignity of one who does not lower their charge: one who exercises responsibility (a bishop, a teacher) must embody this serious gravity. In Titus 2:7, Titus is asked to be "a model of good works, and giving pure, dignified teaching"—his own example must show that the Gospel elevates and ennobles.
3. Finally, it is the tranquil majesty of behavior that pleases God and men: in 1 Timothy 2:2, we pray for "kings and for all those in high positions, that we may lead a peaceful and quiet life, in all godliness and honesty"—this respectable demeanor fosters public peace and trust.
G4587.origine: The word comes from the Greek σεμνός ("respectable, majestic, grave"), which paints the image of a person who commands respect through their presence and demeanor—someone who is literally worthy of respect. This root expresses natural distinction, what stands upright and proud. It is a noble word, used for gods and great figures in ancient Greece.
G4587.emploi: The word appears three times in the New Testament, always in Paul's letters to Timothy and Titus. In 1 Timothy 2:2, it designates how Christians should live under authorities: with seriousness and respect, so that peace may reign. In 1 Timothy 3:4, it is a quality required of elders and deacons, who must govern their households with dignity. In Titus 2:7, it reflects the preaching itself: the teacher must be a model whose respectable person makes the message of the Gospel credible. Paul paints an ideal of Christian life that does not renounce moral nobility but redirects it toward Christ.
G4587.portee: This word invites the believer not to confuse freedom in Christ with looseness or carelessness. Dignity, honesty in behavior, is a means of making the Gospel respectable and accessible—it wins the trust of those who observe us. It is practical wisdom: living soberly, dignified, honors God and creates an atmosphere of peace and trust around oneself.

sens: Roman proconsul of Cyprus
G4588.detail: Sergius Paulus is a Roman magistrate who governs the island of Cyprus for the empire. He is a high-ranking, capable, and educated man. In Acts 13:7, he receives Barnabas and Saul (Paul) and requests to hear their message about God.
G4588.origine: This is a Roman name, Sergius, common among Latin aristocrats. The Bible refers to him by his full title, in the Roman manner: Sergius Paulus, indicating his official status. His surname Paulus suggests a family origin from the region of Latium.
G4588.emploi: Sergius Paulus appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 13:7. This occurs during Paul and Barnabas's first missionary journey to Cyprus. The text presents him as proconsul, meaning Roman governor of this province, and emphasizes that he was an intelligent man who desired to hear the word of God. This brief mention marks the encounter of the Gospel with pagan political power in the Mediterranean world.
G4588.portee: This encounter shows how the Gospel reaches the leaders of the Roman political world, not just the poor or slaves. It demonstrates the power of Christian preaching to engage even educated and respectable authorities.

sens: Son of Adam and Eve, third son mentioned in the biblical genealogy
G4589.detail: Seth is the third son of Adam and Eve, born after the death of Abel. His name means "replacement" or "substituted" in Hebrew, as Eve regarded him as a replacement for the son she had lost (Genesis 4:25). He is the father of Enosh and the ancestor of Noah and all humanity that survived the Flood. In the genealogy of Luke 3:38, he is presented as an important link in the chain of generations connecting Adam to Jesus Christ.
G4589.origine: His Hebrew name שֵׁת (Shèth) comes from a root meaning "to place" or "to establish." Eve herself explains her choice of this name by saying that God has given her a descendant in place of Abel (Genesis 4:25). This name evokes the divine idea of substitution and the continuation of God's plan in the face of the tragedy of the first murder.
G4589.emploi: Seth appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 3:38, at the heart of the genealogy of Jesus established by Luke. This genealogy traces back from Jesus to Adam himself, through the line of Seth. Seth represents the renewal of the human race after sin and murder, and his inclusion underscores the continuity of God's plan through the generations. It is through Seth's lineage that the story of salvation continued.
G4589.portee: Seth's presence in Luke's genealogy reminds the reader that God, despite sin and death, continues His plan of salvation for humanity. It shows that even in the drama of the first murder, God offers restoration and continuation. Jesus, descended from this long lineage beginning with Seth, is presented as the final fulfillment of this uninterrupted divine purpose.

sens: Son of Noah and ancestor of Christ in human genealogy
G4590.detail: Shem is the son of Noah mentioned in the genealogy of Jesus in Luke (Luke 3:36). He is one of the three sons of Noah who survived the Flood and repopulated the earth. As a figure from the Old Testament, Shem embodies an important stage in the divine plan of salvation through human generations.
G4590.origine: The name Shem (שֵׁם in Hebrew) means "name" or "renown." It is a simple term that evokes importance and memory. In the Old Testament, Shem is presented as Noah's firstborn son and the ancestor of the Semitic peoples. His name in Greek, Σήμ, directly reproduces the Hebrew.
G4590.emploi: Shem appears only once in the New Testament: in Luke 3:36, where the evangelist lists the genealogy of Jesus back to Adam. Luke places Shem in the direct lineage between Arphaxad and Noah, thus establishing the genealogical link that connects Jesus to the ancestors of humanity and particularly to the descendants of Noah. This mention links the Savior to the history of salvation from its origins.
G4590.portee: Shem's presence in the genealogy of Jesus reminds the reader that Christ is part of real human history and the divine plan that spans millennia. It shows that the incarnation of the Son of God does not emerge from nothing, but is the culmination of a salvation history where God has never abandoned humanity.

sens: to show or make known something by a sign, gesture, or word
to reveal the future, announce what is to come
to signify, have a meaning or consequence
G4591.detail:
1. To indicate is to show a reality by designating it, notably by a sign or a word that makes it manifest. Jesus "indicated" the kind of death he would die: he did not say it directly, but he signified it through his words, implying what was to happen (John 12:33, John 18:32). It is the same idea when he "indicates" how Peter would glorify God by his death (John 21:19).
2. To announce is to indicate what is to happen in the future. The prophet Agabus "announced" by the Spirit that there would be a great famine (Acts 11:28): he revealed an upcoming event. Similarly, the Revelation is given to "make known" to John the things that must soon take place (Revelation 1:1).
3. Finally, to signify is to have a particular meaning or implication: the word indicates what something means or implies. The three meanings are close: in each case, it is about making something known, either through an enigmatic word, prophecy, or the significance of events.
G4591.origine: The word comes from the Greek σῆμα (sêma), which means "sign." To indicate is thus essentially "to give a sign," "to make a sign." The root evokes the idea of showing something through a visible gesture or a significant word. In the Old Testament, this Greek verb translates several Hebrew verbs that mean "to cry out," "to sound the trumpet," or "to announce"—actions that make something manifest or known.
G4591.emploi: The verb appears 6 times in the New Testament. Three occurrences are found in the Gospel of John (John 12:33, 18:32, 21:19): Jesus "indicates" the nature of his future death or that of Peter, without explicitly naming it. One occurrence is in Acts (Acts 11:28): the prophet Agabus "announces" an upcoming famine through the message of the Spirit. Another in Acts (Acts 25:27) asks Caesar to "indicate" the accusations. The last is in Revelation 1:1, where God "makes known" to John what must soon happen. Everywhere, the word means to make visible, intelligible, or known something that was not: a hidden reality, a future event, a veiled meaning.
G4591.portee: This verb reminds us that God speaks to His prophets and His Church to make known His will and plans. Through the words of Jesus, through the message of the prophets, through Revelation, God indicates to us what is to come and what we must understand. It is a call to attentive listening: God "signifies"; it is up to us to receive what is thus communicated to us.

sens: distinctive mark that allows one to recognize a person or thing
warning or caution
event to come, celestial phenomenon announcing the future
miraculous act manifesting divine power
proof of God's authority or presence
G4592.detail:
1. A mark or signal that allows for the identification of something or someone. For example, Judas's kiss in Matthew 26:48 is a "sign" agreed upon for the soldiers to recognize Jesus. Circumcision in Romans 4:11 is a "sign" of Abraham's covenant with God.

2. A warning or alert message addressed to people. When Jesus says in Matthew 12:39 that "this generation" seeks a "sign," he alludes to a spectacular demonstration meant to prove something to him — but he refuses, as seeking "signs" is also seeking a pretext not to believe.

3. A phenomenon announcing future events: "signs" in the sun, moon, and stars (Luke 21:25) that mark the approach of the end times and God's judgment.

4. A miraculous act — a superhuman action that manifests divine power. The miracles of Jesus in John 2:11 and his other extraordinary acts are "signs" that reveal who he truly is. In Acts 4:16, the Sanhedrin acknowledges that a notable "miracle" has been performed by the apostles.

5. A concrete proof of God's authority or presence. "Signs and wonders" (Acts 2:19, 43) accompany apostolic preaching to show that God is acting. But even false prophets and demons can produce deceptive "signs" (Revelation 13:13-14).
G4592.origine: The Greek word σημεῖον comes from a root meaning "to mark" or "to distinguish." It is fundamentally a visible mark that makes something known. The French words "signe" and "signal" are close heirs. In Hebrew, the word אוֹת (ôt) covers the same field: mark, wonder, miracle. Thus, the Greek translation of the Old Testament regularly renders אוֹת as σημεῖον.
G4592.emploi: The word appears 69 times in the New Testament, largely concentrated in the Gospels and Acts. It primarily denotes a distinctive mark or sign of recognition (Matthew 26:48; Romans 4:11). But its main usage concerns miracles: the extraordinary acts of Jesus are called "signs" because they point to his divine nature and testify to his identity (John 2:11, 23; 6:30). The expression "signs and wonders" (σημεῖα καὶ τέρατα) becomes a formula to designate manifestations of divine power (Acts 2:43; Romans 15:19). The word is also used for celestial phenomena announcing the end times (Luke 21:25; Revelation 12:1, 3), and Jesus warns against the false signs that deceivers will produce (Matthew 24:24; Mark 13:22). An important nuance: the "signs" requested out of unbelief (Matthew 12:38-39) are refused or called to be refused, as believing requires faith, not spectacular proof.
G4592.portee: This word invites the Christian to recognize that God acts visibly in history and manifests himself through powerful acts. The "signs" are not tricks or illusions: they are the authentic traces of divine presence. However, the Bible warns that signs alone do not create faith — a disposition of the heart is necessary. Finally, learning to discern true signs from false ones is learning not to be deceived by deceivers, a permanent challenge for God's people.

sens: Mark something to recognize or remember it
Observe carefully to retain information
Identify someone by spotting them among others
Be cautious of someone to avoid their company
G4593.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to mark: one makes a mark on something or someone to not forget it, as one would note a date on a calendar. It is to record in one's mind or by a visible sign.

2. By extension, "note" means to observe carefully, to look intentionally to retain what one sees. It is to focus attention on a detail or a person.

3. In the context of social spotting, to note someone is to identify them, to recognize them among others — often with a connotation of vigilance or suspicion.

4. In 2 Thessalonians 3:14, Paul asks believers to "note" the one who does not obey his instructions: that is, to spot him, to mark him mentally, so that they can keep him at a distance and that this exclusion may bring him shame. It is an identification for the purpose of disciplinary action.
G4593.origine: The word comes from the family of σημεῖον (semeion), which means "sign" or "mark." To note is therefore to make or apply a mark, to give a distinctive sign. The verb is formed with the suffix -όω which transforms the noun into action. It is a living word in classical Greek and in administrative or scientific texts.
G4593.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament: in 2 Thessalonians 3:14, where Paul uses it in the sense of "marking with a finger," "signaling," "identifying." In this passage, it is a directive for church discipline: the Thessalonians must "note" — that is, spot and observe — the one who refuses to obey the apostle's word, in order not to have dealings with him. The context shows that it is less about simple observation than a collective action aimed at correction through shame. It is a communal act of vigilance and discipline.
G4593.portee: This verse teaches the modern reader that the Christian community has a responsibility: to identify and signal the one who strays from the received teachings, not out of cruelty, but for their amendment. "Noting" invites discernment and honesty: one can only correct what one has first seen and recognized. It is a call to pastoral attention rather than blind condemnation.

sens: The present day, the day one is speaking
This very day, at this precise moment
The present time, the current era
G4594.detail:
1. The word simply designates the day one is in, today. It is the present moment, as opposed to the past or the future: "Give us today our daily bread" (Matthew 6:11) means the bread of this very day, the one we need right now. This concrete sense recurs constantly in the Gospels.

2. The word emphasizes immediacy and urgency: to act or receive something right now, without waiting. Jesus promises the thief: "Today you will be with me in paradise" (Luke 23:43), fixing this moment as the time of deliverance. Or again: "Today I have greatly suffered in dream because of him" (Matthew 27:19), expressing an experience of the very moment.

3. The word can also evoke the present time, the era in which one lives, a historical period: "Until today" means from that moment until the moment one speaks (Romans 11:8). Hebrews 13:8 affirms that Jesus Christ is "the same yesterday and today and forever," contrasting the present time with eternity.
G4594.origine: The Greek word σήμερον comes from a root evoking the very day, what is immediate. In ancient Greek, τήμερον (Attic form) was also found. The word regularly translates the Hebrew יוֹם (day) in the Greek translation of the Old Testament. It is a simple adverb, without significant derivative, that stabilized early in Greek to express the idea of the immediate present.
G4594.emploi: The word appears 41 times in the New Testament, especially in Luke and Matthew (Gospels) and in the epistle to the Hebrews. It is used in the context of prayer (Matthew 6:11), preaching and teaching (Luke 4:21), immediate action (Luke 13:32: "I cast out demons and perform healings today"), and urgent decision (Luke 19:5, 19:9). It often marks the moment of a divine intervention or a decisive encounter. In Acts and the epistle to the Hebrews, it signals the present moment as a time of judgment or call (Acts 4:9, Hebrews 3:7). The word explicitly opposes "tomorrow" (αὔριον) and "yesterday" (χθὲς) to highlight the tension between immediacy and expectation.
G4594.portee: This word reminds the reader that God's will is exercised and realized in the present: God acts "today," he calls "today," and the promise of salvation is offered "today." For the believer, it is a call not to postpone obedience, prayer, or faith. Hebrews 3:7 shows it: "Today, if you hear his voice" — the issue is the present moment, not tomorrow. It is a word of grace and also of spiritual urgency.

sens: Literally: to decompose, to corrupt, to become putrid
Figuratively: to disappear, to lose value, to become useless
G4595.detail:
1. The verb σήπω describes the physical process of decomposition or putrefaction: something deteriorates, rots, disintegrates. In James 5:2, riches are described as 'rotting' — they degrade, lose their solidity, and collapse morally and materially.
2. Figuratively, 'to rot' means to become worthless, to disappear, to nullify. What rots no longer truly exists: it is only destruction. The word paints the image of wealth that was thought to be permanent but evaporates, corrupts, and becomes nothingness.
G4595.origine: The verb σήπω comes from a root expressing decomposition and rot. In the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament), it translates Hebrew verbs such as מָקַק (mâqaq, 'to melt, to dissolve') and כָּלָה (kâlâh, 'to finish, to cease'). The word family always retains the idea of destruction and gradual annihilation.
G4595.emploi: The verb σήπω appears only once in the New Testament: in James 5:2, as a warning against the accumulation of earthly riches. James invites the rich to weep over their rotting wealth — a striking image of material wealth doomed to destruction, unable to survive divine judgment. The context of James is eschatological: the goods of this world are temporary and corruptible, unlike eternal treasures.
G4595.portee: This word invites the reader to redefine their conception of wealth. If money and material possessions inevitably rot, they do not deserve to hold our hearts or our trust. James urges us to seek incorruptible treasures from God, rather than placing our security in what disintegrates. It is a word of freedom: we are freed from the slavery to riches, which are promised to disappear.

sens: precious fabric made from thread produced by the silkworm
garment or object made of silk
luxury item coveted by the rich
G4596.detail:
1. Silk is a fine and shiny fabric, once very rare in the West, obtained by unrolling the cocoon of the silkworm — an invention that came from China and India. In Revelation 18:12, it is listed among the goods of the great city Babylon, alongside gold, silver, and precious stones: this shows that it was a valuable and highly luxurious trade item.
2. The word can refer to both the raw material and the garments or fabrics made from it. The rich and powerful wore silk to display their wealth and status.
3. Spiritually, silk symbolizes earthly wealth, pride, and attachment to the goods of this world — elements that the Bible criticizes when they become idols.
G4596.origine: The Greek word σηρικός comes from the name of the Seres, a people of Asia (probably China) known for producing and exporting silk. That is why the fabric bears the name of this people: it is the characteristic product of the Seres. The word has been borrowed into many ancient and modern languages from Greek.
G4596.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Revelation 18:12. John mentions it in his vision of the destruction of Babylon, the great city symbolizing luxury, idolatry, and the pride of the world rebelling against God. Silk is listed among the goods that the merchants of the world wept over not being able to sell anymore — an indication of the superficial and ephemeral nature of these riches. This apocalyptic context emphasizes the vanity of these earthly goods.
G4596.portee: For the believer, the word silk reminds us that luxury and material wealth, even the most refined, are transient seductions. The vision of their disappearance in divine judgment invites us to turn our hearts away from the riches of this world and fix them on the eternal treasures of God.

sens: Small insect that eats away at fabrics and clothing
Invisible and progressive destruction of material goods
Image of sin or that which corrupts the soul
G4597.detail:
1. The moth is a small insect that feeds on textile fibers: it burrows into clothing and fabrics, gradually eating away at them silently and insidiously. Jesus mentions it in Matthew 6:19 alongside rust as an example of material destruction.
2. Figuratively, the moth represents everything that secretly destroys our earthly riches: while rust corrodes metals, the moth eats away at fabrics, and together they symbolize the inevitable wear of the goods we amass here below. In Matthew 6:20, Jesus contrasts the fate of earthly treasures with the treasures of heaven, which remain intact.
3. In Jesus' teaching, the moth becomes an image of moral corruption: that which eats away at the soul and destroys it from within, as sin ravages the heart of one who serves only money. That is why true treasures should not be sought on earth, but in heaven as stated in Luke 12:33.
G4597.origine: The Greek word σής (sēs) literally refers to the moth of clothing, this tiny but destructive insect. It corresponds in Hebrew to עָשׁ (asch) in Isaiah 50:9 and סָס (sass) in Isaiah 51:8, both having the same meaning. The choice of this small creature to speak of destruction emphasizes that evil often acts silently and secretly, long before one becomes aware of it.
G4597.emploi: The word appears only three times in the New Testament, always in the words of Jesus teaching about riches. In Matthew 6:19-20, it is an element of the Sermon on the Mount: Jesus uses the moth and rust as two symmetrical examples of the vanity of earthly treasures, which naturally degrade. In Luke 12:33, the same teaching returns in a context of sharing goods and almsgiving, where the moth only destroys what one keeps for oneself. In all cases, the word serves to describe a slow, inevitable destruction beyond our control.
G4597.portee: Jesus invites the believer to depend not on material goods, which wear out and disappear, but on God's provision in heaven, which remains eternal. The moth teaches the futility of hoarding: our efforts to accumulate the riches of the world are vain in the face of time passing. Thus, the word pushes us to reevaluate our priorities and place our trust in Christ rather than in earthly riches.

sens: Devoured, damaged by the larvae of the moth
Deteriorated, worn to destruction
Corrupted, degraded (figurative sense)
G4598.detail:
1. The word literally describes what the moth does to fabrics: the larvae of this insect burrow into the cloth and eat away at it, creating holes and rendering it unusable. In James 5:2, the clothes hoarded by the rich are eaten away by moths, symbolizing that no material wealth escapes destruction.
2. Broadly, the word evokes everything that disintegrates, wears out, or rots over time. Accumulated wealth does not last: gold rusts, clothes degrade — everything material is destined to disappear.
3. Spiritually, the word suggests moral corruption or the wear of life without God. What appears solid and precious proves fragile and ephemeral when idolized.
G4598.origine: The Greek word combines two elements: σῆς (the insect called moth, which devours fabrics) and βιβρώσκω (to eat, to devour). It is a striking image from antiquity, where the moth was a well-known scourge of households. The word also appears in ancient Hebrew in Job 13:28, where it describes progressive corruption.
G4598.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in James 5:2, in a critique of materialistic wealth. James denounces the rich who hoard treasures without thinking of God: he lists the scourges that ravage them — the rust that corrodes gold, the moths that eat away at clothing. This accumulation of images of degradation hammers home a message: riches protect no one, they do not last, and those who rely on them are deluded.
G4598.portee: This word invites the Christian not to cling to what rots, what wears out and disappears. It frees from the anxiety of possessing and accumulating, showing that only what is eternal — faith, love, relationship with God — deserves our investment. It is a call to freedom and true wealth.

sens: Make strong physically or morally
Strengthen in faith and perseverance
G4599.detail:
1. Fortify means to make someone strong, capable of enduring effort or suffering. It is to give strength to one who lacks it or who is weakening. The word paints the image of a person receiving new vigor to stand firm.
2. In a spiritual context, to fortify is to strengthen someone in their faith and fidelity. In 1 Peter 5:10, after speaking of the sufferings of Christians, the apostle affirms that God himself will fortify them — that is, he will make them stable and unshakeable in their attachment to Christ, despite the trials that have exhausted them.
G4599.origine: The verb fortify comes from the Greek root σθένος (sthénos), which literally means "strength" or "vigor." It is an uncommon word that expresses the idea of imparting new strength to someone. It belongs to the family of words that express robustness and solidity.
G4599.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Peter 5:10. Peter uses it to announce that God, in his grace, not only forgives and calls Christians, but also makes them able to persevere despite suffering. It is the divine work of stabilizing and strengthening the believer in the face of trials.
G4599.portee: This word reassures us: when we go through difficulties or moments when our faith falters, God does not leave us to ourselves. He actively fortifies us, giving us the moral and spiritual strength to hold on. It is a promise that our weakness is not the end of the story — God himself comes to make us firm and unshakeable.
